cor-cg-finite-termination.title: Finite Termination
cor-cg-finite-termination.html: In exact arithmetic the conjugate gradient iteration reaches r(m)=0, and hence x(m)=x⋆, for some m≤n. If A has only d distinct eigenvalues, then m≤d.

cor-fast-circulant-solve.title: Solving a Circulant System in O(n\log n)
cor-fast-circulant-solve.title_html: Solving a Circulant System in O(nlog⁡n)
cor-fast-circulant-solve.html: Let n=2p, let C∈Mn(C) be an invertible circulant with first row c, and let b∈Cn. Then the solution of Cx=b can be computed in 3C(n)+2n operations.

cor-fast-convolution.title: Convolution in O(n\log n)
cor-fast-convolution.title_html: Convolution in O(nlog⁡n)
cor-fast-convolution.html: Let n=2p. The cyclic convolution c∗d of two vectors in Cn can be computed in 3C(n)+2n=92nlog2⁡n−n+3 operations, where C is as in @thm-fft-cost. Consequently, the product of two polynomials in C[x] of degree at most d can be computed in O(dlog⁡d) operations.

cor-lax-constant-coefficient.title: Constant \B: the flow is conjugation by the exponential
cor-lax-constant-coefficient.title_html: Constant B: the flow is conjugation by the exponential
cor-lax-constant-coefficient.html: Let B∈Mn(C) be a fixed matrix and let L:R→Mn(C) be differentiable with L′=[B,L]. Then L(t)=etBL(0)e−tB(t∈R), so L(t) is similar to L(0) for every t.

cor-pivots-and-minors.title: Pivots Are Ratios of Leading Minors
cor-pivots-and-minors.title_html: Pivots Are Ratios of Leading Minors
cor-pivots-and-minors.html:
Let A∈Mn(F), let 1≤k≤n−1, and write Aj for the leading principal j×j submatrix of A, with detA0:=1.

  1. If the first k pivots of elimination without row swaps are non-zero, then A1,…,Ak are invertible and the j-th pivot equals detAj/detAj−1 for j≤k.
  2. Conversely, if A1,…,An−1 are invertible then elimination without row swaps succeeds on A with non-zero pivots, and A=LU by @thm-lu-exists-without-swaps.

cor-power-method-hermitian.title: Hermitian Matrices: the Rayleigh Quotient Converges Twice as Fast
cor-power-method-hermitian.title_html: Hermitian Matrices: the Rayleigh Quotient Converges Twice as Fast
cor-power-method-hermitian.html: Let A∈Mn(F) be Hermitian, with an orthonormal basis q1,…,qn of eigenvectors, Aqi=λiqi, ordered by modulus so that |λ1|>|λ2|≥⋯≥|λn|. Let x(0)=∑iciqi be a unit vector with c1≠0, and put ρ=|λ2/λ1|. Then for every k, |RA(x(k))−λ1| ≤ Dρ2k,D=1|c1|2∑i≥2|ci|2|λi−λ1|.

cor-rayleigh-frequency-bounds.title: Frequencies from the Rayleigh Quotient
cor-rayleigh-frequency-bounds.html: Let (M,K) be a mass–spring system with natural frequencies ω1≤⋯≤ωn. Then for every j, ωj2=mindim⁡W=j  max0≠v∈W ρ(v)=maxdim⁡W=n−j+1  min0≠v∈W ρ(v), W running over all subspaces of Rn of the stated dimension. In particular ω12=minv≠0ρ(v),ωn2=maxv≠0ρ(v), and every v≠0 gives the upper bound ω12≤ρ(v), with equality exactly when v is a generalized eigenvector for ω1.

def-arithmetic-cost.title: Arithmetic cost of a matrix product
def-arithmetic-cost.title_html: Arithmetic cost of a matrix product
def-arithmetic-cost.html:
Fix a field F and n≥1, and treat the 2n2 entries of A,B∈Mn(F) as indeterminates. A straight-line program is a finite list g1,…,gN in which each gt is either

  1. one of the 2n2 indeterminates, or a constant of F (an input step), or
  2. gr+gs, gr−gs or grgs for some r,s<t (an arithmetic step).

Each gt is then a polynomial in the indeterminates. The program computes the product if for every i,j the polynomial ∑kaikbkj occurs among the gt. Its cost is the number of arithmetic steps, and M(n):=min{cost of a program computing the n×n product} is the arithmetic cost of the n×n product over F.

def-backward-stable.title: Backward stability
def-backward-stable.html: Let f:D→Rm be a problem. An algorithm f^ for f, running in a floating-point model with unit roundoff u, is backward stable if there is a constant c, depending only on the dimensions of the data and not on the data itself or on u, such that for every representable a∈D there exists Δa∈RN with a+Δa∈D,f^(a)=f(a+Δa),‖Δa‖≤cu‖a‖.

def-butterfly-and-twiddle.title: The even-odd permutation, the twiddle matrix and the butterfly
def-butterfly-and-twiddle.title_html: The even-odd permutation, the twiddle matrix and the butterfly
def-butterfly-and-twiddle.html:
Let n=2m with m≥1.

  1. The even-odd permutation matrix Pn∈Mn(C) is the permutation matrix determined by (Pnx)t=x2t,(Pnx)m+t=x2t+1(0≤t≤m−1); it lists the even-numbered entries of x first, then the odd-numbered ones, each in their original order.
  2. The twiddle matrix is Dm:=diag(1,ωn,ωn2,…,ωnm−1)∈Mm(C). Its entries are powers of ωn, not of ωm.
  3. The butterfly matrix is Bn:=(ImDmIm−Dm)∈Mn(C).

def-centered-data-matrix.title: Data matrix, mean and centered data matrix
def-centered-data-matrix.title_html: Data matrix, mean and centered data matrix
def-centered-data-matrix.html: Let x1,…,xN∈Rn. The data matrix is the matrix X∈Mn×N(R) whose j-th column is xj. The mean of the data is x¯:=1N∑j=1Nxj∈Rn, and the centered data matrix is Xc:=X−x¯1⊤∈Mn×N(R), whose j-th column is cj:=xj−x¯.

def-chebyshev-polynomials.title: Chebyshev Polynomials
def-chebyshev-polynomials.html: The Chebyshev polynomials T0,T1,T2,⋯∈R[x] are defined by T0=1,T1=x,Tk+1=2xTk−Tk−1  (k≥1).

def-conjugate-gradient.title: The Conjugate Gradient Iteration
def-conjugate-gradient.html: Let A∈Mn(R) be symmetric positive definite, b∈Rn and x(0)∈Rn. Set r(0)=b−Ax(0),p(0)=r(0). For k=0,1,2,…: if r(k)=0, stop. Otherwise put αk=(r(k))⊤r(k)(p(k))⊤Ap(k),x(k+1)=x(k)+αkp(k),r(k+1)=r(k)−αkAp(k),βk=(r(k+1))⊤r(k+1)(r(k))⊤r(k), and p(k+1)=r(k+1)+βkp(k). This is the conjugate gradient iteration, or CG.

def-dft-matrix.title: The transform matrix
def-dft-matrix.html: For n≥1 let Wn:=nFn∈Mn(C),(Wn)jk=ωnjk(0≤j,k≤n−1), so that c^=Wnc for every c∈Cn.

def-energy-norm.title: The Energy Inner Product and the Energy Norm
def-energy-norm.title_html: The Energy Inner Product and the Energy Norm
def-energy-norm.html: Let A∈Mn(R) be symmetric positive definite. The energy inner product is ⟨x,y⟩A:=y⊤Ax(x,y∈Rn), and the energy norm is ‖x‖A:=⟨x,x⟩A1/2=(x⊤Ax)1/2. Two vectors are A-orthogonal, or conjugate, when ⟨x,y⟩A=0.

def-fiedler-value.title: Fiedler value
def-fiedler-value.html: Let G be a graph on m≥2 vertices with at least one edge. The Fiedler value, or algebraic connectivity, of G is the second smallest eigenvalue μ2(L) of its Laplacian, counted with multiplicity.

def-floating-point-model.title: The floating-point model
def-floating-point-model.html:
A floating-point model consists of a finite set R⊆R of representable numbers with 0,1∈R and −R=R, a map fl:R→R sending each real number to a nearest element of R, and a real number u>0 called the unit roundoff, subject to the following.

  1. (Rounding.) For every t∈R in range, fl(t)=t(1+δ) for some δ with |δ|≤u.
  2. (Arithmetic.) For x,y∈R and ⊙∈{+,−,×,÷} with y≠0 when ⊙ is ÷, the computed value of x⊙y is fl(x⊙y); the computed value of x for x∈R, x≥0, is fl(x). Hence fl(x⊙y)=(x⊙y)(1+δ),|δ|≤u, and likewise fl(x)=x(1+δ) with |δ|≤u.
  3. (No overflow or underflow.) Every quantity occurring in a computation we analyze is assumed to be in range, so that (FP1) applies to it.

def-forward-error.title: Forward and backward error
def-forward-error.html: Let f be a problem, f^ an algorithm for it, and a∈D a representable datum with f(a)≠0. The forward error of f^ at a is the relative error in the answer, ‖f^(a)−f(a)‖‖f(a)‖. The backward error of f^ at a is the smallest relative perturbation of the data that accounts for the computed answer exactly, inf{‖Δa‖‖a‖:a+Δa∈D and f(a+Δa)=f^(a)}, with the convention that it is ∞ when no such Δa exists.

def-generalized-rayleigh-quotient.title: Generalized Rayleigh quotient
def-generalized-rayleigh-quotient.html: Let (M,K) be a mass–spring system. Its generalized Rayleigh quotient is ρ(v):=v⊤Kvv⊤Mv, defined for every v∈Rn with v≠0, and at no other vector.

def-graph-laplacian.title: Graph Laplacian
def-graph-laplacian.html: Let G be a graph with vertices 1,…,m and k≥1 edges, and fix any orientation of G, with incidence matrix N∈Mm×k(R). The Laplacian of G is L:=NN⊤∈Mm(R).

def-growth-factor.title: Growth factor
def-growth-factor.html: Let elimination — with whatever pivoting rule is in force — be run on A∈Mn(R), producing an upper factor U. The growth factor of that run is gn:=maxi,j|uij|maxi,j|aij|, the largest entry in modulus the algorithm produces, relative to the largest entry in modulus it was given. For a run in the model, U means the computed U^.

def-inverse-iteration.title: Inverse Iteration
def-inverse-iteration.html: Let A∈Mn(F), let μ∈F be not an eigenvalue of A, and let x(0) be a unit vector. Inverse iteration with shift μ is the power iteration of @def-power-iteration generated by (A−μI)−1 and x(0); that is, (A−μI)z(k)=x(k),x(k+1)=z(k)‖z(k)‖. The eigenvalue estimates are taken from A itself: μk=(x(k))∗Ax(k).

def-krylov-subspace.title: Krylov Subspace
def-krylov-subspace.html: Let A∈Mn(F), let b∈Fn and let k≥1 be an integer. The k-th Krylov subspace of the pair (A,b) is Kk(A,b):=span(b, Ab, A2b, …, Ak−1b)⊆Fn.

def-lax-pair.title: Lax Pair
def-lax-pair.html: Let I⊆R be an open interval. A Lax pair on I is a pair of functions L,B:I→Mn(C), with L differentiable, such that L′(t)=[B(t),L(t)]:=B(t)L(t)−L(t)B(t)for every t∈I. The equation itself is called a Lax equation, and L is said to flow under it.

def-mass-spring-model.title: The mass–spring model
def-mass-spring-model.html:
1. (Newton’s second law.) A mass mi>0 whose displacement is xi(t) obeys mixi″(t)=fi(t), where fi is the total force on it.
  2. (Hooke’s law.) A spring of stiffness k≥0 whose two ends have moved by a and b pulls its ends together with force k(b−a) acting on the end at a, and −k(b−a) on the end at b. A wall is an end whose displacement is 0. A spring of stiffness 0 exerts no force whatever, so it is the same thing as no spring at all.

def-mass-spring-system.title: Mass–spring system
def-mass-spring-system.html: A mass–spring system with n degrees of freedom is a pair of real symmetric matrices M,K∈Mn(R) with M≻0 and K⪰0, called the mass matrix and the stiffness matrix. A motion of the system is a twice-differentiable function x:R→Rn with Mx″(t)=−Kx(t)for every t∈R.{#eq-mass-spring} The same equation is read for a function x:R→Cn whenever a complex trial solution is convenient; a motion without qualification is real.

def-matrix-multiplication-exponent.title: The exponent of matrix multiplication
def-matrix-multiplication-exponent.html: The exponent of matrix multiplication over F is ω:=inf{τ∈R:M(n)=O(nτ) as n→∞}.

def-mixed-stability.title: Mixed forward-backward stability
def-mixed-stability.html: An algorithm f^ for f:D→Rm is mixed forward-backward stable if there is a constant c, depending only on the dimensions, such that for every representable a∈D there are Δa and Δy with a+Δa∈D and f^(a)=f(a+Δa)+Δy,‖Δa‖≤cu‖a‖,‖Δy‖≤cu‖f(a+Δa)‖.

def-power-iteration.title: Power Iteration
def-power-iteration.html: Let A∈Mn(F) and let x(0)∈Fn with ‖x(0)‖=1. The power iteration generated by A and x(0) is the sequence defined for k≥0 by x(k+1)=Ax(k)‖Ax(k)‖, which is defined as long as Ax(k)≠0, together with the eigenvalue estimates μk=(x(k))∗Ax(k).

def-principal-directions.title: Principal directions and components
def-principal-directions.html: In the situation of @prp-covariance-and-svd, the unit vectors u1,u2,… are the principal directions of the data, and the numbers ui⊤c1,…,ui⊤cN are the i-th principal components: the coordinates of the centered data along ui.

def-qr-iteration.title: The QR Iteration
def-qr-iteration.html: Let A∈Mn(F), where F=R or F=C. Set A(1)=A, and for k≥1 define A(k)=Q(k)R(k),A(k+1)=R(k)Q(k), where A(k)=Q(k)R(k) is a factorization with Q(k)∈Mn(F) unitary and R(k)∈Mn(F) upper triangular. The sequence A(1),A(2),… is the unshifted QR iteration started at A.

def-rayleigh-quotient-iteration.title: Rayleigh Quotient Iteration
def-rayleigh-quotient-iteration.html: Let A∈Mn(F) be Hermitian and let x(0) be a unit vector. Rayleigh quotient iteration is the sequence defined for k≥0 by μk=RA(x(k))=(x(k))∗Ax(k),(A−μkI)z(k)=x(k),x(k+1)=z(k)‖z(k)‖, the step being undefined, and the iteration stopped, when μk is an eigenvalue of A — in which case μk is the answer, exactly.

def-ritz-values.title: Ritz Values and Ritz Vectors
def-ritz-values.html: Let A∈Mn(F), let Qk∈Mn×k(F) have orthonormal columns, and put Hk=Qk∗AQk. The eigenvalues θ1,…,θk of Hk are the Ritz values of A from the subspace span(q1,…,qk), and for an eigenvector y of Hk with Hky=θy and ‖y‖=1, the vector x=Qky is the corresponding Ritz vector; the pair (θ,x) is a Ritz pair.

def-sample-covariance.title: Sample covariance matrix
def-sample-covariance.html: Let x1,…,xN∈Rn with centered data matrix Xc (@def-centered-data-matrix). The sample covariance matrix of the data is S:=1NXcXc⊤∈Mn(R), with entries sab=1N∑j=1N(xaj−x¯a)(xbj−x¯b)(1≤a,b≤n). For w∈Rn with w≠0, the variance of the data in the direction w is the number w⊤Sw/‖w‖2, which for a unit w is w⊤Sw; and the total variance of the data is trS.

def-steepest-descent.title: Steepest Descent
def-steepest-descent.html: Let A≻0 and b∈Rn, and let x(0)∈Rn. Steepest descent is the iteration: for k=0,1,2,…, set r(k)=b−Ax(k); if r(k)=0, stop, since x(k)=x⋆; otherwise put tk=(r(k))⊤r(k)(r(k))⊤Ar(k),x(k+1)=x(k)+tkr(k).

def-toda-flow.title: The Toda Flow
def-toda-flow.html: For M∈Mn(R) write M+ for its strictly upper triangular part and M− for its strictly lower triangular part, so that M is the sum of M−, its diagonal part and M+, and set B(M):=M+−M−. The Toda flow is the Lax equation L′(t)=[B(L(t)), L(t)] for a differentiable L:I→Mn(R) taking symmetric tridiagonal values.

exm-centering-examples.title: Centering three data sets
exm-centering-examples.html:
1. N=4 points in R2: (5,4),(4,1),(2,3),(1,0). Their sum is (12,8), so x¯=(3,2) and Xc=(21−1−22−11−2). Both rows sum to 0.
  2. N=1. Then x¯=x1 and Xc=0: a single point carries no shape at all. This degenerate case matters, because every ratio below has 0/0 here and the statements must exclude it or say what they mean.
  3. Data already centered: if X1=0 then x¯=0 and Xc=X. Centering is idempotent, since Xc1=0 always.

exm-cg-two-eigenvalues.title: Two distinct eigenvalues, two steps
exm-cg-two-eigenvalues.html: Let A=I3+J, where J is the all-ones matrix, let b=e1 and x(0)=0. Run CG.

exm-covariance-examples.html:
1. The four points of @exm-centering-examples (a). Then XcXc⊤=(106610),S=(5/23/23/25/2). Both coordinates have variance 5/2, and the positive off-diagonal entry says they rise and fall together.
  2. Two points ±v in Rn with v≠0, so N=2 and x¯=0. Then XcXc⊤=2vv⊤ and S=vv⊤, of rank one: all the spread is in one direction, and w⊤Sw=(w⊤v)2 vanishes for every w⊥v.

exm-fiedler-two-triangles.html:
Let G have vertices 1,…,6 and edges {1,2}, {1,3}, {2,3}, {3,4}, {4,5}, {4,6}, {5,6}: two triangles joined by a single edge.

exm-growth-attained.html: Let Yn∈Mn(R) have 1 on the diagonal, −1 strictly below it, 0 strictly above it except in the last column, and 1 throughout the last column. For n=4, Y4=(1001−1101−1−111−1−1−11). Run elimination with partial pivoting on Y4 and on Y5, and compute the growth factor of each.

exm-inverse-iteration-2x2.title: Aiming at the smaller eigenvalue
exm-inverse-iteration-2x2.html: Let A=(2112) again, and take the shift μ=34, which is nearer to the eigenvalue 1 than to 3. Run inverse iteration from x(0)=e1, and compare with @exm-power-method-2x2.

exm-lanczos-breakdown.html: Let A=(311131113) and b=e1. Run the Lanczos recurrence of @thm-lanczos, and identify what it finds.

exm-laplacian-two-ways.title: A Laplacian computed twice
exm-laplacian-two-ways.html: Let G be the four-vertex graph of @exr-minors-and-rank-c1: vertices 1,2,3,4 and edges e1={1,2}, e2={2,3}, e3={3,4}, e4={4,1}, e5={1,3}. Compute L from D−A and from NN⊤, and check them against each other.

exm-lax-nilpotent-curve.title: A curve of matrices with a frozen spectrum
exm-lax-nilpotent-curve.title_html: A curve of matrices with a frozen spectrum
exm-lax-nilpotent-curve.html: Take B=(0100) and L0=(0010). Since B2=0, @def-matrix-exponential gives etB=I+tB, and the recipe of the previous example produces L(t)=(1t01)(0010)(1−t01)=(t−t21−t). Three of the four entries move — only the corner ℓ21=1 stands still — and yet trL(t)=0 and detL(t)=−t2+t2=0, so pL(t)(x)=x2 for every t. The curve stays inside one similarity class the whole time.

exm-mass-spring-examples.title: Three systems
exm-mass-spring-examples.html:
1. n=1: one mass m between two walls with springs k1,k2. Then M=(m) and K=(k1+k2), both 1×1.
  2. n=3 with all masses equal to m and all four stiffnesses equal to k. Then M=mI3 and K=kK3, where K3 is the second-difference matrix met in @prp-second-difference-inverse.
  3. The free chain: the same three masses joined to each other by k2,k3 but with no walls, so k1=k4=0. Then K is still symmetric and still B⊤DkB, hence ⪰0, but now K1=0: sliding the whole chain sideways stretches nothing.

exm-matrix-tree-four-vertices.html: For the graph of @exm-laplacian-two-ways, compute detL0 with r=4, and list the spanning trees.
