exm-pca-four-points.html: Take the four points (5,4),(4,1),(2,3),(1,0) of @exm-centering-examples (a). Find the mean, the sample covariance matrix, the principal directions, the best-fitting line, the total squared distance to it, and the fraction of variance it explains.

exm-pinning-the-chain.title: Pinning the middle mass
exm-pinning-the-chain.html: In @exm-three-mass-chain with k=m=1, hold mass 2 fixed. Deleting row and column 2 from K3 and from I3 gives K′=diag(2,2) and M′=I2, so the pinned frequencies are μ1=μ2=2. The unpinned ones are 2−2≈0.765, 2≈1.414 and 2+2≈1.848, and indeed 0.765≤1.414≤1.414≤1.414≤1.848, which is @prp-pinning-interlaces, here with two of the four inequalities equalities. The answer is also visible: with the middle mass pinned, the two outer masses no longer interact, and each is a single mass between two unit springs, of frequency 2.

exm-power-method-2x2.title: Every iterate exactly
exm-power-method-2x2.html: Let A=(2112) and x(0)=e1. Compute Ake1, the estimates μk, and the errors, in closed form.

exm-power-method-cyclic.title: The method that never converges
exm-power-method-cyclic.html: Let P∈M3(R) be the cyclic permutation matrix of @exm-cyclic-permutation, with columns e2,e3,e1, so that P(x1,x2,x3)=(x3,x1,x2). Run the power iteration from x(0)=e1 and from x(0)=114(1,2,3).

exm-qr-fixed-points.title: Two matrices the iteration cannot move
exm-qr-fixed-points.title_html: Two matrices the iteration cannot move
exm-qr-fixed-points.html: Determine the QR iterates of A=diag(3,1) and of the rotation B=(0−110).

exm-qr-three-steps.title: The subdiagonal shrinking at the predicted rate
exm-qr-three-steps.title_html: The subdiagonal shrinking at the predicted rate
exm-qr-three-steps.html: Run the unshifted QR iteration on the symmetric tridiagonal matrix A=(210121012), whose eigenvalues are 2+2, 2 and 2−2. Carry out the first step exactly, and tabulate three steps.

exm-rayleigh-estimate-lowest-mode.title: Guessing the lowest mode of the chain
exm-rayleigh-estimate-lowest-mode.title_html: Guessing the lowest mode of the chain
exm-rayleigh-estimate-lowest-mode.html: For the chain of @exm-three-mass-chain with k=m=1, estimate ω12 by guessing a shape, without computing any eigenvalue.

exm-ritz-diagonal.title: Ritz values closing in on the extremes
exm-ritz-diagonal.title_html: Ritz values closing in on the extremes
exm-ritz-diagonal.html: Let A=diag(4,3,2,1) and b=(1,1,1,1). Compute the Lanczos coefficients, the Ritz values for k=1,2,3, and the residual of the largest Ritz pair at k=3.

exm-rotation-stuck.title: The unshifted algorithm on a rotation
exm-rotation-stuck.title_html: The unshifted algorithm on a rotation
exm-rotation-stuck.html: Let B=(0−110). Explain why no unshifted QR iteration can bring B closer to triangular form, and say which hypothesis of @thm-qr-convergence fails.

exm-rqi-2x2.title: Three steps, exactly
exm-rqi-2x2.html: Run Rayleigh quotient iteration on A=(2112) from x(0)∝(2,1), in exact arithmetic.

exm-schur-complement-by-elimination.title: Two steps, two Schur complements
exm-schur-complement-by-elimination.html: Let A=(123275−148). Carry out two steps of elimination without row swaps, then compute A/A1 and A/A2 directly from @def-schur-complement, and check @thm-elimination-is-schur-complements in both cases.

exm-shift-repairs-rotation.title: The shift repairs the rotation, and deflates a symmetric example
exm-shift-repairs-rotation.title_html: The shift repairs the rotation, and deflates a symmetric example
exm-shift-repairs-rotation.html:
1. Apply one shifted QR step with μ=i to B=(0−110).
  2. Apply one shifted QR step with μ=2 to the symmetric tridiagonal matrix A with diagonal (2,2,2) and off-diagonal entries 1.

exm-six-digit-model.title: The model we compute in
exm-six-digit-model.html: Throughout this chapter, a worked number comes from the six-digit decimal model: R is the set of numbers ±d1.d2d3d4d5d6×10e with digits di, d1≠0 and e in some fixed finite range, together with 0; and fl rounds to the nearest such number. (The range of e is what (FP3) lets us stop thinking about.) What is u, and what is fl(99999996)?

exm-steepest-descent-sharp.title: The bound is attained
exm-steepest-descent-sharp.html: Let A=diag(9,1), b=(9,1) and x(0)=(2,−8). Run three steps of steepest descent and compare with @thm-steepest-descent.

exm-strassen-small-entry.title: A small entry lost entirely
exm-strassen-small-entry.html: Work in binary arithmetic with 53-bit significands, rounding to nearest, so that u=2−53. Verify the hypotheses of @thm-strassen-not-entrywise-stable for ε=2−27, and say what each algorithm returns for the (2,2) entry of the product of A=B=diag(1,2−27).

exm-strassen-two-by-two.title: Seven products on integer data
exm-strassen-two-by-two.html: Multiply A=(1234) and B=(5678) by @thm-strassen, with blocks of size 1, so that each Pk is a number. Check against the classical product.

exm-three-mass-chain.title: Three equal masses, four equal springs
exm-three-mass-chain.title_html: Three equal masses, four equal springs
exm-three-mass-chain.html: Take n=3 with every mass m and every stiffness k, so that M=mI3 and K=kK3 as in @exm-mass-spring-examples (b). Find the natural frequencies and the normal modes of @thm-normal-modes.

exm-toda-two-by-two.title: The 2 \times 2 flow, twice
exm-toda-two-by-two.title_html: The 2×2 flow, twice
exm-toda-two-by-two.html:
Let n=2, so L=(d1e1e1d2) and @eq-toda-coordinates reads d1′=2e12,d2′=−2e12,e1′=e1(d2−d1).

  1. Verify by hand that trL and detL are constant along the flow.
  2. Solve the flow explicitly for L(0)=(0110).

exr-conjugate-gradient-a1.title: A1
exr-conjugate-gradient-a1.html:
1. Define the energy inner product of a symmetric positive definite A, and say which clause of @def-positive-semidefinite makes it an inner product.
  2. State @prp-quadratic-minimizer, and explain in one sentence why it makes ‖⋅‖A the natural yardstick for the error.
  3. State the optimality property of the k-th conjugate gradient iterate, naming the set over which it is optimal.
  4. Determine whether the following statement is correct, and justify your answer: in exact arithmetic, conjugate gradients applied to a 1000×1000 positive definite matrix with 5 distinct eigenvalues terminates after at most 5 steps.
  5. Write down the two Chebyshev facts of @lem-chebyshev-extremal, and say which of the two supplies the κ in @thm-cg-convergence.

exr-conjugate-gradient-b1.title: B1: Steepest descent by hand
exr-conjugate-gradient-b1.html:
Let A=(2001), b=(2,1) and x(0)=(0,0).

  1. Compute x(1) and x(2) by steepest descent.
  2. Compute ‖x(k)−x⋆‖A2 for k=0,1,2 and compare the ratios with the bound of @thm-steepest-descent.

exr-conjugate-gradient-b2.title: B2: Conjugate gradients by hand
exr-conjugate-gradient-b2.html: Let A=(4113), b=(1,2) and x(0)=(0,0). Run conjugate gradients to termination, and verify at each stage that the residuals are orthogonal and the directions A-orthogonal.

exr-conjugate-gradient-b3.title: B3: Chebyshev by recurrence
exr-conjugate-gradient-b3.html:
1. Compute T5 from @def-chebyshev-polynomials.
  2. Evaluate T5(1), T5(−1) and T5(0), and check them against @lem-chebyshev-extremal (a).
  3. Evaluate T5(2) from the polynomial, and check it against the closed formula of @lem-chebyshev-extremal (b).

exr-conjugate-gradient-c1.title: C1: Sharpness of Kantorovich
exr-conjugate-gradient-c1.html:
Let a≥c>0 and let A=diag(a,c).

  1. Prove that for y=(1,1) the inequality of @lem-kantorovich is an equality.
  2. Hence deduce that the constant (κ−1)/(κ+1) in @thm-steepest-descent cannot be replaced by any smaller one.

exr-conjugate-gradient-c2.title: C2: Finite termination, from polynomials
exr-conjugate-gradient-c2.html: Give a second proof of the second statement of @cor-cg-finite-termination — that d distinct eigenvalues force termination in at most d steps — using @eq-cg-polynomial-min instead of a dimension count. Hint: consider q(x)=∏i=1d(1−x/μi).

exr-conjugate-gradient-c3.title: C3: What preconditioning does to the spectrum
exr-conjugate-gradient-c3.title_html: C3: What preconditioning does to the spectrum
exr-conjugate-gradient-c3.html:
Let A,M∈Mn(R) be symmetric positive definite and write M=CC⊤ with C invertible, which is possible by @thm-cholesky.

  1. Prove that C−1AC−⊤ is symmetric positive definite.
  2. Prove that C−1AC−⊤ and M−1A are similar, and deduce that their eigenvalues coincide.
  3. Hence show that those eigenvalues are exactly the generalized eigenvalues of the pencil A−λM in the sense of @def-generalized-eigenvalue, and say what @thm-cg-convergence then predicts for preconditioned conjugate gradients.

exr-elimination-pivoting-and-cost-a1.title: A1
exr-elimination-pivoting-and-cost-a1.html:
1. Define a flop and the growth factor gn.
  2. State the partial pivoting rule, and say what @prp-partial-pivoting-bounds-multipliers gets from it.
  3. State the leading term of the flop count for an LU factorization, for two triangular solves and for Cholesky.
  4. Decide whether each statement is correct, with a reason: (i) “a triangular solve needs pivoting when the diagonal entries are small”; (ii) “elimination with partial pivoting is backward stable”; (iii) “a backward stable factorization gives an accurate solution”.
  5. In one sentence, what does @thm-elimination-is-schur-complements say about the trailing block after k steps?

exr-elimination-pivoting-and-cost-b1.title: B1: A Schur complement by two routes
exr-elimination-pivoting-and-cost-b1.title_html: B1: A Schur complement by two routes
exr-elimination-pivoting-and-cost-b1.html:
Let A=(21−145−1−282).

  1. Carry out one step of elimination without row swaps and read off the trailing 2×2 block.
  2. Compute A/A1=D−Ca11−1B directly from @def-schur-complement and check that the two agree.
  3. Carry out the second step and verify @cor-pivots-and-minors (a) by computing detA1, detA2 and detA3.

exr-elimination-pivoting-and-cost-b2.title: B2: Growth, with and without a swap
exr-elimination-pivoting-and-cost-b2.title_html: B2: Growth, with and without a swap
exr-elimination-pivoting-and-cost-b2.html:
Let A=(10−4111), and work in the six-digit decimal model.

  1. Factor A without an exchange, compute g2, and compute L^U^ exactly.
  2. Do the same after exchanging the rows.
  3. Compare the two backward errors with the bound of @eq-lu-growth-bound.

exr-elimination-pivoting-and-cost-b3.title: B3: The Cholesky entry bound
exr-elimination-pivoting-and-cost-b3.html:
Let A=(4−26−25−16−126), whose Cholesky factor was computed in @exm-cholesky-by-hand to be L with rows (2,0,0), (−1,2,0), (3,1,4).

  1. Check @thm-cholesky-stability (a) entry by entry.
  2. Compute |L||L⊤| and check that every entry is at most maxp,q|apq|.
  3. What would the bound of @eq-lu-growth-bound require if A were factored by general elimination with partial pivoting instead?

exr-elimination-pivoting-and-cost-c1.title: C1: Column diagonal dominance needs no pivoting
exr-elimination-pivoting-and-cost-c1.title_html: C1: Column diagonal dominance needs no pivoting
exr-elimination-pivoting-and-cost-c1.html:
Call A∈Mn(R) strictly column diagonally dominant if |ajj|>∑i≠j|aij| for every j.

  1. Show that partial pivoting makes no exchange at the first step.
  2. Show that A/A1 is again strictly column diagonally dominant, and that each of its column sums ∑i≥2|aij′| is at most the corresponding column sum ∑i≥1|aij| of A.
  3. Deduce that elimination without any exchanges succeeds and that gn<2.

Hint: for (c), bound every entry of every A(k) by a column sum of A.

exr-elimination-pivoting-and-cost-c2.title: C2: The growth bound is attained for every n
exr-elimination-pivoting-and-cost-c2.title_html: C2: The growth bound is attained for every n
exr-elimination-pivoting-and-cost-c2.html:
Let Yn be the matrix of @exm-growth-attained: yii=1, yij=−1 for i>j, yin=1 for all i, and yij=0 for j>i with j<n.

  1. Prove that partial pivoting makes no exchange at any step, and that every multiplier equals −1.
  2. Prove by induction on k that after k steps the active trailing block is again of the form Yn−k, except that its last column is 2k times the all-ones vector.
  3. Deduce gn=2n−1, and explain why this does not contradict the practical success of partial pivoting.

exr-fast-matrix-multiplication-a1.title: A1
exr-fast-matrix-multiplication-a1.html:
1. State how many arithmetic operations @def-matrix-multiplication uses for the product of two n×n matrices, separating multiplications from additions.
  2. Define the exponent ω, and state what is proved about it in this section.
  3. True or false: @thm-strassen shows that M(2)≤7. Justify your answer.
  4. Which properties of m×m matrices does the proof of @thm-strassen use? Say what would go wrong if the identity had needed two blocks to commute.
  5. State the difference between the error bound of @prp-classical-product-entrywise and that of @prp-strassen-norm-bound, and say for which matrices the difference matters.

exr-fast-matrix-multiplication-b1.title: B1: Seven products by hand
exr-fast-matrix-multiplication-b1.html: Let A=(2−103) and B=(14−21). Compute P1,…,P7 of @thm-strassen with blocks of size 1, assemble the four entries, and check the answer against @exm-matrix-multiplication. Hence state how many multiplications and how many additions you performed.

exr-fast-matrix-multiplication-b2.title: B2: One block, one level
exr-fast-matrix-multiplication-b2.html: Let A=(1021011011020211),B=(1201011020111101), partitioned into 2×2 blocks. Compute P3 and P5 of @thm-strassen, hence the (1,2) block of AB, and verify it against the block formula A11B12+A12B22.

exr-fast-matrix-multiplication-b3.title: B3: Counting the recursion
exr-fast-matrix-multiplication-b3.html:
Let n=2p.

  1. How many multiplications does the recursion of @thm-strassen-cost perform, as a function of p? How many does the classical recipe perform?
  2. Using T(n)=7nlog2⁡7−6n2, compute T(n) and 2n3−n2 for n=8 and n=64.
  3. Hence say, for these two sizes, which recipe uses fewer operations.

exr-fast-matrix-multiplication-c1.title: C1: Would twenty-three products for three-by-three beat Strassen?
exr-fast-matrix-multiplication-c1.title_html: C1: Would twenty-three products for three-by-three beat Strassen?
exr-fast-matrix-multiplication-c1.html:
Suppose a ring identity multiplies two 3×3 matrices with q>9 multiplications of combinations of entries, together with some fixed number of additions, and is used recursively on 3×3 block matrices.

  1. Show that the recursion performs qp multiplications on matrices of size n=3p, and deduce that it gives ω≤log3⁡q.
  2. You are given that such an identity exists with q=23; this is a result of Laderman, which is not proved here. Determine whether recursing on it beats @thm-strassen-cost. Justify your answer.
  3. Determine the largest q for which such an identity would beat @thm-strassen-cost.

Hint: compare logarithms to a common base.

exr-fast-matrix-multiplication-c2.title: C2: Where the entrywise bound really fails
exr-fast-matrix-multiplication-c2.title_html: C2: Where the entrywise bound really fails
exr-fast-matrix-multiplication-c2.html:
Let ε>0 and A=B=(1εεε).

  1. Compute AB and |A||B| exactly, and identify the entry of AB that is smallest as ε→0.
  2. Compute P1,…,P7 exactly, and find which of them is largest as ε→0.
  3. Suppose ε,2ε,1−ε,1+ε,1+2ε and 2ε2 are representable, and that the model rounds (1+ε)2 to 1+2ε and (ε−1)(1+ε) to −1, each time losing a trailing ε2. Determine c^22, and the least constant c for which |C^−AB|≤cu|A||B| can hold at the (2,2) position.

Hint: with ε=2−27 in 53-bit binary arithmetic, both roundings are what rounding to nearest does.

exr-fast-matrix-multiplication-c3.title: C3: Only the products recurse
exr-fast-matrix-multiplication-c3.html:
Suppose someone proposes an identity that multiplies 2×2 matrices with eight multiplications but only two additions, and recurses on it.

  1. Write down the recurrence for its operation count with T(1)=1, and solve it exactly for n=2p.
  2. Hence determine the exponent it gives, and compare with @thm-strassen-cost.
  3. Explain in one sentence what part of an identity the exponent depends on.

exr-floating-point-and-backward-error-a1.title: A1
exr-floating-point-and-backward-error-a1.html:
1. State the three clauses of @def-floating-point-model, and say which one is an exclusion rather than an assumption about accuracy.
  2. Define the unit roundoff, and give its value for a decimal model carrying t significant digits.
  3. Define the forward error and the backward error of an algorithm at a datum, and say which of the two a user can usually measure.
  4. Decide whether each statement is correct, with a reason: (i) “a backward stable algorithm returns an answer with small forward error”; (ii) “if the computed x^ has a tiny residual, then x^ is close to x”.
  5. Why is @def-floating-point-model called a model rather than a theorem?

exr-floating-point-and-backward-error-b1.title: B1: The \gamma calculus
exr-floating-point-and-backward-error-b1.title_html: B1: The γ calculus
exr-floating-point-and-backward-error-b1.html:
Assume (j+k)u<1.

  1. Prove that 1+γk=1/(1−ku).
  2. Hence prove that γj+γk+γjγk≤γj+k.
  3. Explain in one sentence why (b) is the statement one needs when two separately analyzed computations are performed one after the other.

exr-floating-point-and-backward-error-b2.title: B2: Summation
exr-floating-point-and-backward-error-b2.html:
Let x1,…,xn be representable, let nu<1, and let sn be computed by s1=x1, sk=fl(sk−1+xk).

  1. Prove that sn=∑k=1nxk(1+θk) with |θk|≤γn−1.
  2. Deduce |sn−∑kxk|≤γn−1∑k|xk|, and explain why this is not a bound on the relative error of sn.
  3. Give three representable numbers in the six-digit model for which the computed sum has relative error larger than u.

exr-floating-point-and-backward-error-b3.title: B3: The model by hand
exr-floating-point-and-backward-error-b3.html:
Work in the six-digit decimal model.

  1. Compute fl(1/3) and verify (FP1) for it.
  2. Compute the two sides of fl(fl(a+b)+c) and fl(a+fl(b+c)) for a=105, b=1, c=1, and say what this shows about the model.

exr-floating-point-and-backward-error-c1.title: C1: When backward stability says nothing
exr-floating-point-and-backward-error-c1.title_html: C1: When backward stability says nothing
exr-floating-point-and-backward-error-c1.html:
Let x,y∈Rn and let sn be the computed inner product of @thm-inner-product-backward-error.

  1. Prove that |sn−x⊤y|≤γn|x|⊤|y|, where |⋅| is entrywise.
  2. Deduce that if all xiyi≥0 then the relative error of sn is at most γn.
  3. Give x,y∈R3 with representable entries, in the six-digit model, for which the relative error of sn is at least 1. Explain why this does not contradict @thm-inner-product-backward-error.

exr-floating-point-and-backward-error-c2.title: C2: An unstable way to compute a variance
exr-floating-point-and-backward-error-c2.title_html: C2: An unstable way to compute a variance
exr-floating-point-and-backward-error-c2.html:
Given x1,…,xN with mean x―=1N∑ixi, the quantity S=∑i(xi−x―)2 can be computed in one pass as S=∑ixi2−1N(∑ixi)2, or in two passes by forming x― first.

  1. Verify the identity ∑i(xi−x―)2=∑ixi2−1N(∑ixi)2.
  2. In the six-digit model, run both routes on x=(10000,10001,10002), showing every operation, and compare with the exact value S=2.
  3. Say which route is to be preferred and why, in the vocabulary of this section.

exr-graph-laplacians-a1.title: A1
exr-graph-laplacians-a1.html:
1. Define the Laplacian of a graph, and say why it does not depend on the orientation used to define it.
  2. Write down the formula for x⊤Lx as a sum over edges, and deduce that L⪰0.
  3. State the matrix-tree theorem, including all its hypotheses.
  4. True or false: a graph on m vertices is connected if and only if rankL=m−1. Justify your answer.
  5. True or false: if L has eigenvalue 0 with multiplicity 1, then detL0>0. Justify your answer.

exr-graph-laplacians-b1.title: B1: The four-cycle
exr-graph-laplacians-b1.html:
Let C4 be the graph on vertices 1,2,3,4 with edges {1,2},{2,3},{3,4},{4,1}.

  1. Write down L and explain why it is a circulant in the sense of @def-circulant.
  2. Find all eigenvalues of L, the Fiedler value, and a Fiedler vector.
  3. Compute detL0 and list the spanning trees.

exr-graph-laplacians-b2.title: B2: Counting trees in a bowtie
exr-graph-laplacians-b2.title_html: B2: Counting trees in a bowtie
exr-graph-laplacians-b2.html:
Let G have vertices 1,…,5 and edges {1,2},{1,3},{2,3},{3,4},{3,5},{4,5}: two triangles sharing the vertex 3.

  1. Write down L and compute detL0 with r=1.
  2. Count the spanning trees directly, and check that the two answers agree.
  3. Verify that x=(1,1,0,−1,−1) is an eigenvector of L, and say what its eigenvalue tells you.

exr-graph-laplacians-b3.title: B3: Which minors are \pm 1?
exr-graph-laplacians-b3.title_html: B3: Which minors are ±1?
exr-graph-laplacians-b3.html:
Let G be the graph on vertices 1,2,3 with edges e1={1,2}, e2={2,3}, e3={1,3}, e4={1,2} (so e1 and e4 are parallel). Orient every edge from the smaller vertex to the larger, let r=3 and I={1,2}.

  1. Write down N and N0=NI,[4].
  2. Compute detNI,S for all six sets S of two edges, and say in each case whether S is a spanning tree.
  3. Hence find the number of spanning trees, and check it against detL0.

exr-graph-laplacians-c1.title: C1: Cayley’s formula
exr-graph-laplacians-c1.html:
Let Km be the complete graph on m≥2 vertices, in which every pair of distinct vertices is joined by exactly one edge, and let Jt∈Mt(R) be the all-ones matrix.

  1. Show that the Laplacian of Km is mIm−Jm, and that L0=mIm−1−Jm−1 for every choice of deleted vertex.
  2. Prove that det(mIm−1−Jm−1)=mm−2.
  3. Deduce Cayley’s formula: Km has exactly mm−2 spanning trees. Check it for m=2,3,4 against a direct count.

Hint for (b): the eigenvalues of Jt are visible from its rank and its row sums.

exr-graph-laplacians-c2.title: C2: Weighted graphs
exr-graph-laplacians-c2.html:
Give each edge e of a graph G on m≥2 vertices a weight we>0, let W=diag(w1,…,wk), and define the weighted Laplacian Lw:=NWN⊤, with N the incidence matrix of any orientation.

  1. Prove that x⊤Lwx=∑ewe(xue−xve)2, and deduce that Lw⪰0 with the same kernel as L.
  2. Prove the weighted matrix-tree theorem: for any vertex r, detL0w=∑T ∏e∈Twe, the sum running over all spanning trees T of G.
  3. Check (b) on the graph of @exm-laplacian-two-ways by comparing the coefficient of w1w2w3 on both sides, and confirm that setting every we=1 recovers @thm-matrix-tree.

Hint for (b): NWN⊤=(NW1/2)(NW1/2)⊤.

exr-krylov-subspaces-a1.title: A1
exr-krylov-subspaces-a1.html:
1. Define Kk(A,b) and state its dimension in terms of mA,b.
  2. State the Arnoldi identity of @thm-arnoldi (b), naming the shape of every matrix in it.
  3. True or false: for Hermitian A, the Arnoldi process needs all of q1,…,qj to produce qj+1. Justify your answer.
  4. What does a breakdown hk+1,k=0 mean, and why is it good news?
  5. Give the formula for the residual of a Ritz pair, and say why it costs nothing to evaluate.

exr-krylov-subspaces-b1.title: B1: Dimensions
exr-krylov-subspaces-b1.html:
For each pair (A,b), determine dim⁡Kk(A,b) for every k≥1. Justify your answer.

  1. A=diag(2,2,5), b=(1,1,1).
  2. A=diag(2,2,5), b=(1,−1,0).
  3. A=(0100), b=e2.
  4. A the 4×4 matrix with Aej=ej+1 for j≤3 and Ae4=0, b=e1.

exr-krylov-subspaces-b2.title: B2: Two Arnoldi steps
exr-krylov-subspaces-b2.html: Let A=(211021001),b=e3. Carry out two Arnoldi steps. Write down Q2, H~2 and H2, verify @eq-arnoldi, and compute the two Ritz values with their residuals. Hence say which, if either, is a converged eigenvalue estimate.

exr-krylov-subspaces-b3.title: B3: Lanczos on a tridiagonal matrix
exr-krylov-subspaces-b3.title_html: B3: Lanczos on a tridiagonal matrix
exr-krylov-subspaces-b3.html: Let A∈Mn(R) be symmetric tridiagonal with every subdiagonal entry non-zero, and let b=e1. Prove that the Lanczos process produces qj=±ej for every j, and hence that Tn=A up to signs. What does this say about the cost of Lanczos on a matrix that is already tridiagonal?

exr-krylov-subspaces-c1.title: C1: Ritz values from the other end
exr-krylov-subspaces-c1.title_html: C1: Ritz values from the other end
exr-krylov-subspaces-c1.html:
Let A∈Mn(C) be Hermitian and let θ1(k)≥⋯≥θk(k) be the Ritz values from Kk(A,b), 1≤k≤d.

  1. Prove that θk(k) is non-increasing in k and that θk(k)≥λn(A).
  2. Deduce a bound for θk(k)−λn(A) from @thm-ritz-extreme-convergence, with no new argument.
  3. Show that at k=d the Ritz values are d of the eigenvalues of A, and say which.

exr-krylov-subspaces-c2.title: C2: Shift invariance, and what it costs
exr-krylov-subspaces-c2.title_html: C2: Shift invariance, and what it costs
exr-krylov-subspaces-c2.html:
Let A∈Mn(F), b≠0, and let σ,c∈F with c≠0.

  1. Prove that Kk(cA+σI,b)=Kk(A,b) for every k.
  2. Deduce that the Arnoldi vectors qj are the same for A and for cA+σI, up to a scalar of modulus one, and that the Ritz values transform by θ↦cθ+σ.
  3. Contrast this with Section 5: explain in two sentences why shifting accelerates the QR algorithm but does not accelerate a Krylov method, and what one must do instead to get the effect.

exr-krylov-subspaces-c3.title: C3: When the Krylov space is everything
exr-krylov-subspaces-c3.title_html: C3: When the Krylov space is everything
exr-krylov-subspaces-c3.html:
Let A∈Mn(F).

  1. Prove that there exists b with Kn(A,b)=Fn if and only if mA=pA.
  2. Prove that in that case the Arnoldi process run to k=n produces a unitary Qn with Qn∗AQn upper Hessenberg, all of whose subdiagonal entries are non-zero.
  3. Hence give a second proof of @thm-hessenberg-form over C for such A, and explain why it does not replace Chapter 10’s.

Hint for (a): Chapter 9 §05 calls such a b a cyclic vector.

exr-lax-pairs-and-the-toda-flow-a1.title: A1
exr-lax-pairs-and-the-toda-flow-a1.html:
1. Define a Lax pair, and say which of the two functions is required to be differentiable.
  2. State @thm-lax-isospectral, and name the two results from earlier chapters its proof uses.
  3. Determine whether the following statement is correct, and justify your answer: if L′=[B,L] then L(t)=L(0) for all t.
  4. Explain in one sentence why the proof of @thm-lax-isospectral does not construct the conjugating matrix S(t).
  5. Write down the Toda equations @eq-toda-coordinates for n=3, and check that the sum of the three diagonal equations is 0.

exr-lax-pairs-and-the-toda-flow-b1.title: B1: A Lax pair verified
exr-lax-pairs-and-the-toda-flow-b1.html:
Let B=(0100) and L(t)=(t−t21−t).

  1. Verify directly that L′(t)=[B,L(t)].
  2. Compute pL(t) and confirm @thm-lax-isospectral in this case.
  3. Determine whether L(t) and L(0) are similar for every t, and exhibit the similarity.

exr-lax-pairs-and-the-toda-flow-b2.title: B2: The bracket by hand
exr-lax-pairs-and-the-toda-flow-b2.html: Let L=(12023101−1). Compute B(L) and [B(L),L] directly, and check the answer against @prp-toda-equations.

exr-lax-pairs-and-the-toda-flow-b3.title: B3: One QR step on an exponential
exr-lax-pairs-and-the-toda-flow-b3.title_html: B3: One QR step on an exponential
exr-lax-pairs-and-the-toda-flow-b3.html:
Let L0=(0110) and A(1)=eL0.

  1. Show that etL0=(c(t)s(t)s(t)c(t)) with c(t)=12(et+e−t) and s(t)=12(et−e−t).
  2. Find the QR factorization of etL0 with positive diagonal, and hence L(t)=Q(t)⊤L0Q(t).
  3. Compare your L(1) with @exm-toda-two-by-two (b).

exr-lax-pairs-and-the-toda-flow-c1.title: C1: The power sums are constants of the motion
exr-lax-pairs-and-the-toda-flow-c1.title_html: C1: The power sums are constants of the motion
exr-lax-pairs-and-the-toda-flow-c1.html:
Let (L,B) be a Lax pair on I.

  1. Prove that t↦tr(L(t)m) is constant for every integer m≥1. Hint: the product rule, then @thm-trace-properties (3).
  2. Deduce, for n=2, that the characteristic polynomial of L(t) is constant, without using @thm-lax-isospectral.

exr-lax-pairs-and-the-toda-flow-c2.title: C2: How far \B is from being determined
exr-lax-pairs-and-the-toda-flow-c2.title_html: C2: How far B is from being determined
exr-lax-pairs-and-the-toda-flow-c2.html:
Let (L,B) be a Lax pair on I and let C:I→Mn(C) satisfy [C(t),L(t)]=0 for every t.

  1. Prove that (L,B+C) is also a Lax pair.
  2. Give an example with C≠0, and conclude that a Lax equation does not determine B.
  3. Prove, using @lem-skew-upper-splitting, that there is nevertheless exactly one skew-symmetric B for which B+ (upper triangular) equals a given symmetric L — that is, the B(L) of @def-toda-flow is the only natural candidate once “skew-symmetric” and “upper triangular” are the two slots.

exr-lax-pairs-and-the-toda-flow-c3.title: C3: Symmetry constrains \B
exr-lax-pairs-and-the-toda-flow-c3.title_html: C3: Symmetry constrains B
exr-lax-pairs-and-the-toda-flow-c3.html:
Let (L,B) be a Lax pair of real matrices on I with L(t) symmetric for every t.

  1. Prove that [B(t)+B(t)⊤, L(t)]=0 for every t.
  2. Deduce that (L,12(B−B⊤)) is also a Lax pair, so that B may always be taken skew-symmetric.
  3. Determine whether the Toda B(L) of @def-toda-flow satisfies the hypothesis of (a). Justify your answer.

exr-numerical-least-squares-a1.title: A1
exr-numerical-least-squares-a1.html:
1. Define θ for a least-squares problem Az≈b with rankA=n, and say what θ=0 means about the system.
  2. State @thm-least-squares-conditioning, and say which of its two terms survives when the residual is zero.
  3. Explain in one sentence why κ2(A)2 appears in the normal-equation route even for a consistent system, and why it need not appear in the reflection route.
  4. True or false: “a matrix with κ2(A)=103 should never be handled by the normal equations”. Justify your answer.
  5. What quantity does @thm-householder-backward-stable bound, and which quantity does it not depend on?

exr-numerical-least-squares-b1.title: B1: Reading the bound
exr-numerical-least-squares-b1.html:
Let A∈M50×3(R) have κ2(A)=105, and suppose the data are accurate to ε=10−10 relatively. Using @eq-ls-first-order with u≈10−16 where needed:

  1. Bound the relative error of the exact least-squares solution caused by the data error, when the residual is zero.
  2. Do the same when tan⁡θ=1.
  3. In case (b), how many digits does the normal-equation route lose on top of the data error, and how many does a backward stable method lose?

exr-numerical-least-squares-b2.title: B2: Where the product goes singular
exr-numerical-least-squares-b2.title_html: B2: Where the product goes singular
exr-numerical-least-squares-b2.html:
Let A=(11ε00ε) as in @exm-normal-equations-fail, in the model with u=2−53.

  1. For which ε does fl(1+ε2)=1 hold, and what is fl(A⊤A) then?
  2. Express the threshold in (a) in terms of κ2(A) and u.
  3. Explain why the reflection route is untroubled at that threshold.

exr-numerical-least-squares-b3.title: B3: One reflection, by hand
exr-numerical-least-squares-b3.html:
Let x=(3,0,4)∈R3.

  1. Compute w and w′ as in @thm-householder-maps-vector, and the two amplification factors ‖x‖/‖w‖ and ‖x‖/‖w′‖.
  2. Verify the identity ‖w‖2‖w′‖2=4‖x‖2‖x~‖2 on this example.
  3. Is the sign choice important for this x? Justify your answer.

exr-numerical-least-squares-c1.title: C1: The squared term is attained
exr-numerical-least-squares-c1.title_html: C1: The squared term is attained
exr-numerical-least-squares-c1.html:
Let ε,δ>0 and take A=(100ε00),b=(10δ),E=(000001),f=0.

  1. Compute κ2(A), the least-squares solution x, the residual r and tan⁡θ.
  2. Using (∗) in the proof of @thm-least-squares-conditioning, compute x′(0) exactly.
  3. Hence show that the squared term of @thm-least-squares-conditioning is attained, in the sense that ‖x′(0)‖/‖x‖ equals κ2(A)2εAtan⁡θ exactly, and explain what this says about any algorithm for this problem.

exr-numerical-least-squares-c2.title: C2: Why the residual has to appear
exr-numerical-least-squares-c2.title_html: C2: Why the residual has to appear
exr-numerical-least-squares-c2.html:
Let A∈Mm×n(F) have rank n, and let x+=A+b be the least-squares solution, where A+ is the pseudoinverse of @def-pseudoinverse.

  1. Prove that A+=(A∗A)−1A∗ when rankA=n, and deduce ‖A+‖=1/σn(A).
  2. Deduce from (∗) in the proof of @thm-least-squares-conditioning that if E=0 — only b is perturbed — then no κ2(A)2 term can appear, whatever the residual.
  3. Explain, in one or two sentences, why perturbing A is different: which term of (∗) carries the residual, and why it cannot be present when E=0.

exr-numerical-least-squares-c3.title: C3: A reflection applied to a matrix
exr-numerical-least-squares-c3.title_html: C3: A reflection applied to a matrix
exr-numerical-least-squares-c3.html:
Let H=Hw be a Householder reflection in Rm and let A∈Mm×n(R).

  1. Using @thm-householder-backward-stable (b) and ‖M‖≤‖M‖F≤n‖M‖ for M∈Mm×n, show that the computed B^ satisfies ‖B^−HA‖≤(10m+16)nu‖A‖.
  2. Deduce that σi(B^) differs from σi(A) by at most (10m+16)nu‖A‖ for every i. Hint: Chapter 19 §10 or Chapter 16 §09 bounds the perturbation of singular values by the norm of the perturbation.
  3. Explain why the corresponding statement is false for the classical Gram–Schmidt process, citing @exm-gram-schmidt-loses-orthogonality.

exr-power-method-and-inverse-iteration-a.title: A1
exr-power-method-and-inverse-iteration-a.html:
1. State the two hypotheses of @thm-power-method on the eigenvalues and on the starting vector, and say what the rate ρ is.
  2. For a Hermitian A, at what rate does the eigenvector converge and at what rate does the Rayleigh quotient? Which earlier result explains the relation between the two?
  3. Explain in one sentence why inverse iteration with shift μ finds the eigenvalue nearest μ.
  4. True or false: “the shifted matrix in inverse iteration is nearly singular, so the method is unreliable”. Justify your answer.
  5. Give the per-step cost of the power method, of inverse iteration and of Rayleigh quotient iteration, for a dense n×n matrix.

exr-power-method-and-inverse-iteration-b.title: B1: A rate, read off the spectrum
exr-power-method-and-inverse-iteration-b.title_html: B1: A rate, read off the spectrum
exr-power-method-and-inverse-iteration-b.html:
Let A=(4123).

  1. Find the eigenvalues and eigenvectors of A, and the rate ρ of the power method.
  2. Starting from x(0)=e1, compute Ake1 in closed form and verify that the direction converges at rate ρk.
  3. How many steps are needed to gain six decimal digits?

exr-power-method-and-inverse-iteration-b.title: B2: Choosing a shift
exr-power-method-and-inverse-iteration-b.html:
Let A=diag(10,3,1).

  1. What is the rate of the plain power method?
  2. Find the rate of inverse iteration with shift μ=0, and say which eigenvector it finds.
  3. Find the rate of inverse iteration with shift μ=52, and say which eigenvector it finds.
  4. Which shift would you choose to compute the middle eigenvalue as fast as possible, and what rate does it give? Explain why no shift gives a rate of 0.

exr-power-method-and-inverse-iteration-b.title: B3: Deflating a symmetric matrix
exr-power-method-and-inverse-iteration-b.html:
Let A=(2112).

  1. Write down A′=A−3q1q1⊤ for the unit eigenvector q1 of the eigenvalue 3, and verify its eigenvalues directly.
  2. What does the power method of @thm-power-method, applied to A′ from x(0)=e1, produce, and at what rate?
  3. Explain why the answer to (b) makes deflation look better than it is.

exr-power-method-and-inverse-iteration-c.title: C1: What the squaring really needs
exr-power-method-and-inverse-iteration-c.title_html: C1: What the squaring really needs
exr-power-method-and-inverse-iteration-c.html:
Let A∈Mn(F) be Hermitian with orthonormal eigenbasis q1,…,qn, and let x be a unit vector with s=‖x−q1q1∗x‖.

  1. Prove that |RA(x)−λ1|≤s2maxi≠1|λi−λ1|.
  2. Show by example that the corresponding statement for a non-Hermitian A is false: exhibit A∈M2(C), an eigenvalue λ1 with unit eigenvector q1, and unit vectors x with s→0 for which |x∗Ax−λ1| is not O(s2).
  3. Hence say which hypothesis of @thm-rqi-cubic the example violates, and which step of the proof breaks.

exr-power-method-and-inverse-iteration-c.title: C2: Two eigenvalues of equal modulus, over the reals
exr-power-method-and-inverse-iteration-c.title_html: C2: Two eigenvalues of equal modulus, over the reals
exr-power-method-and-inverse-iteration-c.html:
Let A∈M2(R) be the rotation matrix (0−110).

  1. Find the eigenvalues of A and explain why @thm-power-method does not apply.
  2. Describe the power iteration from an arbitrary unit x(0)∈R2, and show that no line is a limit.
  3. Now take the shift μ=12 and run inverse iteration over C. Does the theorem apply? Compute ρμ. Hint: the eigenvalues of A are ±i.
  4. Deduce a one-sentence moral about which of the two failures of @exm-power-method-cyclic a shift can repair.

exr-power-method-and-inverse-iteration-c.title: C3: A small residual certifies an eigenpair
exr-power-method-and-inverse-iteration-c.title_html: C3: A small residual certifies an eigenpair
exr-power-method-and-inverse-iteration-c.html:
Let A∈Mn(C) be Hermitian with orthonormal eigenbasis q1,…,qn, let q^ be a unit vector, let μ^=RA(q^) and ε=‖Aq^−μ^q^‖. Suppose λj is the only eigenvalue of A in the interval (μ^−g,μ^+g).

  1. Prove that ‖q^−qjqj∗q^‖≤ε/g, assuming ε<g.
  2. Deduce a bound on |μ^−λj| from @thm-kato-temple, and compare it with the bound from @thm-hermitian-residual-bound.
  3. In the inverse iteration of @def-inverse-iteration with a backward stable solve, ε is about 1/‖z^‖+cu‖A−μI‖. Explain what (a) then says about the computed direction, and in particular why the accuracy improves as the shift improves.

exr-principal-components-a1.title: A1
exr-principal-components-a1.html:
1. Define the centered data matrix and the sample covariance matrix, and say what w⊤Sw means for a unit vector w.
  2. State @thm-best-fitting-affine-subspace, including the value of the minimum and the claim about the mean.
  3. True or false: the principal directions of a data set are the eigenvectors of XX⊤. Justify your answer.
  4. True or false: if N=3 points in R10 are given, then S has rank at most 2. Justify your answer.
  5. Why should a computation of the principal directions avoid forming XcXc⊤?

exr-principal-components-b1.title: B1: A four-point cloud
exr-principal-components-b1.html:
The points (1,1),(3,5),(5,3),(7,7) are given in R2.

  1. Compute x¯, Xc, XcXc⊤ and S.
  2. Find the singular values of Xc and the principal directions.
  3. Find the best-fitting line, the total squared distance to it, and the fraction of variance it explains. Verify the total squared distance directly.

exr-principal-components-b2.title: B2: Variance direction by direction
exr-principal-components-b2.html: For the data of Exercise B1, compute the variance in the directions e1, e2, 12(1,1) and 12(1,−1), and say which of them is largest and why that was predictable.

exr-principal-components-b3.title: B3: Changing the units
exr-principal-components-b3.html:
The centered data matrix of a two-coordinate data set is Xc=(3−300004−4). The second coordinate is then re-expressed in units c times smaller, which multiplies row 2 by c>0.

  1. Find the principal directions before the change.
  2. Find the value of c at which the first principal direction switches from one coordinate axis to the other, and say what happens exactly at that value.

exr-principal-components-c1.title: C1: The mean is forced, and the projection is not a shortcut
exr-principal-components-c1.title_html: C1: The mean is forced, and the projection is not a shortcut
exr-principal-components-c1.html:
Let x1,…,xN∈Rn with mean x¯.

  1. Prove that the point p∈Rn minimizing ∑j‖xj−p‖2 is unique and equals x¯. (This is the case k=0, which @thm-best-fitting-affine-subspace excludes, so it has to be proved rather than quoted.)
  2. Hence deduce that for every subspace U, the affine subspace p+U minimizing D over translates of U is x¯+U.
  3. Give an example of data and a subspace U for which x¯+U is not the best-fitting affine subspace of its dimension, so that the choice of U still matters.

exr-principal-components-c2.title: C2: Total variance is a trace, and what that buys
exr-principal-components-c2.title_html: C2: Total variance is a trace, and what that buys
exr-principal-components-c2.html:
Let x1,…,xN∈Rn with sample covariance S, and let Q∈Mn(R) be orthogonal.

  1. Prove that the data Qx1,…,QxN have sample covariance QSQ⊤, and deduce that the total variance trS is unchanged.
  2. Prove that for any orthonormal basis (q1,…,qn) of Rn, the sum of the variances of the data in the n directions qi equals trS.
  3. Deduce that no orthonormal frame can make every coordinate variance small: some qi always has variance at least trS/n. For the data of @exm-pca-four-points, which frames attain that bound?

exr-the-fast-fourier-transform-a1.title: A1
exr-the-fast-fourier-transform-a1.html:
1. Write down the matrix Wn, and say how it is related to the Fourier matrix Fn of Chapter 11.
  2. State @thm-fft-factorization, and say what each of the three factors on the right costs to apply.
  3. How many operations does Wnx cost as a plain matrix–vector product, and how many by the fast algorithm when n=2p?
  4. True or false: the fast Fourier transform computes a different transform from the one in Chapter 11, which is why it is faster. Justify your answer.
  5. Why does the algorithm require n to be a power of two, and what is done when it is not?

exr-the-fast-fourier-transform-b1.title: B1: A transform of length four
exr-the-fast-fourier-transform-b1.title_html: B1: A transform of length four
exr-the-fast-fourier-transform-b1.html:
Let c=(1,1,−1,−1)∈C4.

  1. Compute W4c by the procedure of this section, showing the two halves and the twiddles.
  2. Check the answer by evaluating the symbol pc at the fourth roots of unity.
  3. Count the operations your computation in (a) used, and compare with C(4).

exr-the-fast-fourier-transform-b2.title: B2: A transform of length eight
exr-the-fast-fourier-transform-b2.title_html: B2: A transform of length eight
exr-the-fast-fourier-transform-b2.html: Let c=(2,1,0,3,2,1,0,3)∈C8. Compute W8c by the procedure, showing both levels, and verify entry j=2 directly from @def-dft-matrix.

exr-the-fast-fourier-transform-b3.title: B3: A product of polynomials by convolution
exr-the-fast-fourier-transform-b3.title_html: B3: A product of polynomials by convolution
exr-the-fast-fourier-transform-b3.html:
Let p=1+2x+3x2 and q=2+x in C[x].

  1. What is the smallest power of two n for which the recipe in the proof of @cor-fast-convolution is valid? Write down the padded coefficient vectors c and d.
  2. Compute c∗d directly from the definition of cyclic convolution, and read off pq.
  3. Show that using n=3 instead would give the wrong answer, and identify which coefficient wraps onto which.

exr-the-fast-fourier-transform-c1.title: C1: Splitting into three
exr-the-fast-fourier-transform-c1.html:
Let n=3m with m≥1, let ωn=e2πi/n, and for s=0,1,2 let u(s):=Wm(xs, x3+s, …, x3(m−1)+s)∈Cm.

  1. Prove that for 0≤q≤2 and 0≤i≤m−1, (Wnx)qm+i=∑s=02ω3qsωnisui(s), where ω3=e2πi/3.
  2. Deduce a recursive procedure for n=3p, and show that its cost C3 satisfies C3(3m)≤3C3(m)+12m and hence C3(3p)≤4p3p=4nlog3⁡n.

Hint for (a): imitate the proof of @thm-fft-factorization, splitting the index k by its remainder modulo 3 and using ωn3=ωm and ωnm=ω3.

exr-the-fast-fourier-transform-c2.title: C2: The fourth power of the transform
exr-the-fast-fourier-transform-c2.title_html: C2: The fourth power of the transform
exr-the-fast-fourier-transform-c2.html:
Let n≥1 and let Rn∈Mn(C) be the permutation matrix with (Rn)jl=1 when j+l≡0(modn) and 0 otherwise, so that (Rnx)j=xn−j with the subscript read modulo n.

  1. Prove that Wn2=nRn.
  2. Deduce that Wn4=n2In and Fn4=In, and that every eigenvalue of Fn lies in {1,i,−1,−i}.
  3. Deduce a second proof that Wn−1=1nWn―.

exr-the-qr-algorithm-a1.title: A1
exr-the-qr-algorithm-a1.html:
1. Write down one step of the unshifted QR iteration, and one step of the shifted one, and prove in one line each that both are similarities.
  2. State @thm-qr-is-orthogonal-iteration, and say in one sentence what it has to do with the power method.
  3. True or false: the QR iterates of a matrix always converge to an upper triangular matrix. Justify your answer.
  4. Why is the iteration run on an upper Hessenberg matrix rather than on a full one? Give the two costs.
  5. In @prp-exact-shift-deflates, which hypothesis on Z is doing the work, and where exactly is it used?

exr-the-qr-algorithm-b1.title: B1: One step by hand
exr-the-qr-algorithm-b1.html: Let A=(2112). Compute the QR factorization of A in the sense of @thm-qr-factorization, then A(2)=RQ. Verify that A(2) is symmetric, has trace 4 and determinant 3, and that its off-diagonal entry is smaller than that of A. Hence estimate how many steps are needed to make the off-diagonal entry smaller than 10−3.

exr-the-qr-algorithm-b2.title: B2: Fixed points
exr-the-qr-algorithm-b2.html:
Determine which of the following matrices are fixed points of the unshifted QR iteration, that is, satisfy A(2)=A(1). Justify your answer; for those that are not, name what changes.

  1. any upper triangular A with positive real diagonal entries;
  2. any unitary A;
  3. A=(0110);
  4. any normal A.

exr-the-qr-algorithm-b3.title: B3: A shift that deflates
exr-the-qr-algorithm-b3.html: Let Z=(1234). Take μ to be either eigenvalue of Z and carry out one shifted QR step. Verify the conclusion of @prp-exact-shift-deflates. Hint: you need only the last row of R.

exr-the-qr-algorithm-c1.title: C1: Hessenberg form is not enough by itself
exr-the-qr-algorithm-c1.title_html: C1: Hessenberg form is not enough by itself
exr-the-qr-algorithm-c1.html:
1. Prove that if Z is upper Hessenberg with zm+1,m=0 for some 1≤m≤n−1, then spec(Z)=spec(Z11)∪spec(Z22), where Z11 is the leading m×m block and Z22 the trailing (n−m)×(n−m) block.
  2. Deduce that a QR implementation may, at every step, replace the problem by two smaller ones as soon as one subdiagonal entry vanishes.
  3. Give a 3×3 upper Hessenberg matrix with no zero subdiagonal entry for which the unshifted iteration never reduces any subdiagonal entry at all.

exr-the-qr-algorithm-c2.title: C2: Hermitian iterates and the Rayleigh quotient
exr-the-qr-algorithm-c2.title_html: C2: Hermitian iterates and the Rayleigh quotient
exr-the-qr-algorithm-c2.html:
Let A∈Mn(C) be Hermitian and let A(k) be its unshifted QR iterates.

  1. Prove that every A(k) is Hermitian with the same eigenvalues as A.
  2. Prove that ann(k)=RA(un(k)), where un(k) is the last column of Uk−1 and RA is the Rayleigh quotient of @def-rayleigh-quotient.
  3. Hence explain, citing @thm-hermitian-residual-bound, why the Rayleigh shift μk=ann(k) is a certified eigenvalue estimate, and say what the certificate is.

exr-the-qr-algorithm-c3.title: C3: Why the powers are the right object
exr-the-qr-algorithm-c3.title_html: C3: Why the powers are the right object
exr-the-qr-algorithm-c3.html:
Let A∈Mn(C) be invertible, with unshifted QR iterates as in @def-qr-iteration.

  1. Prove that for 1≤j≤n, the subspace spanned by the first j columns of Uk equals Ak(span(e1,…,ej)).
  2. Deduce that if the first j columns of Uk converge to a basis of an A-invariant subspace W, then the entries of A(k+1) in rows j+1,…,n of columns 1,…,j tend to 0.

Hint for (b): write the entries as inner products of A applied to one column against another.

exr-vibrations-a1.title: A1
exr-vibrations-a1.html:
1. State the two hypotheses on M and K in @def-mass-spring-system, and say which one guarantees that ρ(v) is defined for every v≠0.
  2. State @thm-normal-modes (b), including the normalization of the eigenvectors.
  3. A system has K invertible. What does @thm-normal-modes say about ω1? What if K is singular?
  4. True or false: if every stiffness ke of a chain is doubled and every mass is left alone, every natural frequency is multiplied by 2. Justify your answer.
  5. True or false: for M=diag(1,4) the squared natural frequencies are the eigenvalues of K divided by 1 and by 4 in some order. Justify your answer.

exr-vibrations-b1.title: B1: Two masses, two springs
exr-vibrations-b1.html:
A cart of mass 2 is joined to a wall by a spring of stiffness 2, and a cart of mass 1 is joined to the first cart by a spring of stiffness 1; the second cart is free on the right.

  1. Write down M and K.
  2. Find the natural frequencies and an M-orthonormal basis of normal modes.
  3. Verify directly that the two modes are M-orthogonal but not orthogonal for the standard inner product.

exr-vibrations-b2.title: B2: Bounding the slowest mode
exr-vibrations-b2.html: For the system of Exercise B1, estimate ω12 from above using the guesses g=(1,1) and g=(2,3), and compare with the exact value.

exr-vibrations-b3.title: B3: Stiffening a chain
exr-vibrations-b3.html:
In the system of Exercise B1, the stiffness of the second spring is increased from 1 to 2, so that K becomes K′=(4−2−22).

  1. Verify that K′⪰K.
  2. Compute the new squared frequencies and check @prp-frequency-monotonicity (a).

exr-vibrations-c1.title: C1: The free chain drifts
exr-vibrations-c1.html:
Let (M,K) be a mass–spring system.

  1. Prove that ω1=0 if and only if K is singular, and that in that case the generalized eigenvectors for ω=0 are exactly the non-zero vectors of kerK.
  2. Hence describe all motions of the free chain of @exm-mass-spring-examples (c) with three equal masses m and equal inner stiffnesses k, given that kerK is spanned by 1.
  3. Deduce that the total momentum ∑imixi′(t) of the free chain is constant in time.

exr-vibrations-c2.title: C2: Adding a mass cannot raise a frequency, and can lower it a lot
exr-vibrations-c2.title_html: C2: Adding a mass cannot raise a frequency, and can lower it a lot
exr-vibrations-c2.html:
1. Let (M,K) be a mass–spring system and let t>0. Prove that the system (M+tepep⊤,K), obtained by adding mass t to the p-th degree of freedom, has ωj′(t)≤ωj for every j, and that t↦ωj′(t) is non-increasing.
  2. For the single mass of @exm-mass-spring-examples (a) with m=k1=k2=1, compute ω1′(t) exactly and find limt→∞ω1′(t).
  3. Give an example of a mass–spring system and a p for which adding mass at p leaves the largest frequency unchanged. Hint: look for a mode that does not move the p-th mass.

lem-chebyshev-extremal.title: Chebyshev Polynomials: Size Inside and Growth Outside
lem-chebyshev-extremal.title_html: Chebyshev Polynomials: Size Inside and Growth Outside
lem-chebyshev-extremal.html:
For every k≥0 and every w∈C∖{0}, Tk(w+w−12)=wk+w−k2.{#eq-chebyshev-substitution} Consequently:

  1. |Tk(x)|≤1 for every real x∈[−1,1], and Tk(1)=1;
  2. for every real z>1, Tk(z)=12((z+z2−1)k+(z+z2−1)−k) ≥ 12(z+z2−1)k, and, separately, Tk(z)≥1.

lem-gamma-bound.title: Accumulated rounding
lem-gamma-bound.html: Let k≥1 and let δ1,…,δk satisfy |δi|≤u, and let ρ1,…,ρk∈{+1,−1}. If ku<1, then ∏i=1k(1+δi)ρi=1+θwith|θ|≤γk:=ku1−ku.

lem-incidence-minors-unimodular.title: Unimodularity of Incidence Minors
lem-incidence-minors-unimodular.html:
Let N∈Mm×k(R) be the incidence matrix of an oriented graph G with m vertices and k≥1 edges. Write ne∈Rm for the column of N belonging to the edge e.

  1. Every square submatrix of N has determinant 0, 1 or −1.
  2. For a set S of edges, the list (ne)e∈S is linearly independent if and only if S contains no cycle.
  3. Fix a vertex r and put I=[m]∖{r}. For a set S of exactly m−1 edges, S is a spanning tree of G if and only if it contains no cycle, and detNI,S={±1if S is a spanning tree of G,0otherwise.

lem-kantorovich.title: Kantorovich’s Inequality
lem-kantorovich.html: Let A∈Mn(R) be symmetric positive definite with eigenvalues λ1≥⋯≥λn>0. Then for every y∈Rn, (y⊤Ay)(y⊤A−1y)≤(λ1+λn)24λ1λn(y⊤y)2.

lem-mean-minimizes-spread.title: Distance to a flat, and where its translate wants to be
lem-mean-minimizes-spread.title_html: Distance to a flat, and where its translate wants to be
lem-mean-minimizes-spread.html:
Let U⊆Rn be a subspace, let Q=In−PU be the orthogonal projection onto U⊥, and let p∈Rn.

  1. For every x∈Rn,  d(x,p+U)=‖Q(x−p)‖, and the nearest point of p+U exists.
  2. For points x1,…,xN with mean x¯, ∑j=1N‖Q(xj−p)‖2=∑j=1N‖Q(xj−x¯)‖2+N‖Q(x¯−p)‖2. In particular the left side is smallest exactly when x¯∈p+U.

lem-scalar-oscillator.title: The scalar oscillator
lem-scalar-oscillator.html: Let ω≥0 and let y:R→C be twice differentiable with y″=−ω2y. If ω>0, then y(t)=y(0)cos⁡ωt+y′(0)ωsin⁡ωt for every t; if ω=0, then y(t)=y(0)+y′(0)t. Conversely every function of these two shapes satisfies y″=−ω2y.

lem-skew-upper-splitting.title: Skew plus upper triangular, uniquely
lem-skew-upper-splitting.html: Every M∈Mn(R) is M=K+U for exactly one skew-symmetric K and one upper triangular U. If M is symmetric then K=M−−M+=−B(M).

lem-substitution-row.title: One Row of Substitution
lem-substitution-row.html: Let m≥0, let t1,…,tm, y1,…,ym, c and d≠0 be representable, and suppose s0=c,sp=fl(sp−1−fl(tpyp))(p=1,…,m),z=fl(sm/d) are computed in the model of @def-floating-point-model, with (m+1)u<1. Then there are θ0,…,θm with c=dz(1+θ0)+∑p=1mtpyp(1+θp),|θp|≤γm+1  for all p. If the final division is omitted, so that z=sm, the same identity holds with d=1 and |θp|≤γm.

prp-classical-product-entrywise.title: The classical product has a small entrywise error
prp-classical-product-entrywise.title_html: The classical product has a small entrywise error
prp-classical-product-entrywise.html: Let A,B∈Mn(R) have representable entries, let nu<1, and let C^ be the product computed by @def-matrix-multiplication, each entry as one inner product taken in the natural order. Then |C^−AB| ≤ γn|A||B| entrywise.

prp-covariance-and-svd.title: The Covariance Matrix and the Singular Value Decomposition
prp-covariance-and-svd.title_html: The Covariance Matrix and the Singular Value Decomposition
prp-covariance-and-svd.html:
Let Xc∈Mn×N(R) be a centered data matrix with singular values σ1≥σ2≥… (padded with zeros to length n), and let Xc=UΣV⊤ be a singular value decomposition with columns u1,…,un of U. Put S=1NXcXc⊤. Then:

  1. S is symmetric and S⪰0;
  2. Sui=σi2Nui for every i, so the eigenvalues of S are σ12/N≥⋯≥σn2/N and the ui are an orthonormal eigenbasis;
  3. for every w≠0, the variance of the data in the direction w is the Rayleigh quotient RS(w) of @def-rayleigh-quotient;
  4. trS=1N∑j=1N‖xj−x¯‖2=1N∑iσi2.

prp-exact-shift-deflates.title: An Exact Shift Deflates in One Step
prp-exact-shift-deflates.title_html: An Exact Shift Deflates in One Step
prp-exact-shift-deflates.html: Let Z∈Mn(F) be upper Hessenberg, n≥2, with all its subdiagonal entries zi+1,i non-zero — such a matrix is called unreduced, the word @lem-tridiagonal-eigenvector-ends used for the tridiagonal case. Let μ∈F be an eigenvalue of Z. Let Z−μI=QR with Q unitary and R upper triangular, and put Z′=RQ+μI. Then the last row of R is zero, and the last row of Z′ is μen⊤. In particular zn,n−1′=0 and znn′=μ.

prp-fiedler-edge-monotone.title: Adding an Edge Raises No Eigenvalue
prp-fiedler-edge-monotone.title_html: Adding an Edge Raises No Eigenvalue
prp-fiedler-edge-monotone.html: Let G be a graph on m vertices with at least one edge, and let G′ be G with one extra edge joining u≠v. Then L′=L+ww⊤ with w=eu−ev, and μj(L′) ≥ μj(L)(j=1,…,m). In particular the Fiedler value does not decrease when an edge is added.

prp-fiedler-minimum.title: The Fiedler Value as a Minimum
prp-fiedler-minimum.title_html: The Fiedler Value as a Minimum
prp-fiedler-minimum.html: Let G be a graph on m≥2 vertices with at least one edge. Then μ2(L)=min{x⊤Lxx⊤x : x∈Rm, x≠0, x⊤1=0}, and the minimum is attained at an eigenvector for μ2(L).

prp-fiedler-positive-iff-connected.title: Positive Fiedler Value Means Connected
prp-fiedler-positive-iff-connected.html: Let G be a graph on m≥2 vertices with at least one edge. Then μ2(L)>0 if and only if G is connected.

prp-frequency-monotonicity.title: Stiffening Raises, Loading Lowers
prp-frequency-monotonicity.html:
Let (M,K) and (M′,K′) be mass–spring systems with n degrees of freedom, with natural frequencies ωj and ωj′.

  1. If M′=M and K′⪰K, then ωj′≥ωj for every j.
  2. If K′=K and M′⪰M, then ωj′≤ωj for every j.

prp-hessenberg-preserved.title: A QR Step Preserves Hessenberg Form
prp-hessenberg-preserved.title_html: A QR Step Preserves Hessenberg Form
prp-hessenberg-preserved.html: Let Z∈Mn(R) be upper Hessenberg, n≥2. Then Z has a factorization Z=QR with Q orthogonal and R upper triangular in which Q is a product of n−1 Givens rotations and is itself upper Hessenberg; and for this factorization RQ is again upper Hessenberg. Producing R and then RQ costs about 6n2 flops.

prp-krylov-properties.title: Krylov Spaces: Nesting, Dimension, Invariance
prp-krylov-properties.html:
Let A∈Mn(F) and b∈Fn with b≠0, and let d=deg⁡mA,b≥1 be the degree of the A-annihilator of b (@def-t-annihilator). Then, for every k≥1:

  1. Kk(A,b)={p(A)b:p∈F[x], deg⁡p≤k−1}, and Kk⊆Kk+1 and AKk⊆Kk+1;
  2. dim⁡Kk(A,b)=min(k,d);
  3. Kk+1=Kk if and only if k≥d, and in that case Kk=Z(b;A) is A-invariant.

prp-laplacian-basic.title: First Properties of the Laplacian
prp-laplacian-basic.html:
Let G be a graph on m vertices with k≥1 edges and Laplacian L. Then:

  1. L=D−A; in particular L is symmetric and does not depend on the orientation chosen in @def-graph-laplacian.
  2. For every x∈Rm, x⊤Lx=∑e=1k(xue−xve)2, where ue and ve are the two ends of the edge e. Consequently L⪰0.
  3. L1=0, where 1=(1,…,1)∈Rm.

prp-lu-cost.title: The Cost of Elimination
prp-lu-cost.html:
Counting each of the five operations as one flop, and counting only arithmetic on matrix and vector entries:

  1. Elimination without row swaps on A∈Mn(R) costs n(n−1)(4n+1)6=23n3−12n2−16n flops, that is 23n3+O(n2).
  2. Forward substitution with a unit lower triangular L costs n2−n flops and back substitution with an upper triangular U costs n2, so solving Ax=b from a factorization costs 2n2−n flops.
  3. The Cholesky recursion of Chapter 12 §02 on a positive definite A∈Mn(R) costs n(n+1)(2n+1)6=13n3+12n2+16n flops, that is 13n3+O(n2), of which n are square roots.

prp-omega-at-least-two.title: The exponent is at least two
prp-omega-at-least-two.title_html: The exponent is at least two
prp-omega-at-least-two.html: M(n)≥n2 for every n≥1, and therefore ω≥2.

prp-partial-pivoting-bounds-multipliers.title: Partial Pivoting Bounds the Multipliers
prp-partial-pivoting-bounds-multipliers.html: Run elimination with partial pivoting: at step k, before eliminating, exchange row k with a row r≥k for which |ark(k−1)| is largest. Then every multiplier satisfies |ℓik|≤1, in exact arithmetic; and in the model |ℓ^ik|≤1 as well.

prp-pinning-interlaces.title: Pinning Interlaces the Frequencies
prp-pinning-interlaces.html: Let (M,K) be a mass–spring system with n≥2 degrees of freedom and natural frequencies ω1≤⋯≤ωn. Fix p, let I={1,…,n}∖{p}, and let M′=MI,I and K′=KI,I be the principal submatrices on I. Then (M′,K′) is a mass–spring system with n−1 degrees of freedom, and its natural frequencies μ1≤⋯≤μn−1 satisfy ωj ≤ μj ≤ ωj+1(1≤j≤n−1).

prp-qr-iteration-similar.title: Every Step Is a Unitary Similarity
prp-qr-iteration-similar.title_html: Every Step Is a Unitary Similarity
prp-qr-iteration-similar.html: In the notation of @def-qr-iteration, A(k+1)=(Q(k))∗A(k)Q(k) for every k. Consequently all the matrices A(k) are unitarily similar to A, and they share its characteristic polynomial, its eigenvalues with multiplicities, its trace and its determinant.

prp-quadratic-minimizer.title: The Solution Minimizes the Energy Functional
prp-quadratic-minimizer.title_html: The Solution Minimizes the Energy Functional
prp-quadratic-minimizer.html: Let A∈Mn(R) be symmetric positive definite, b∈Rn, and define ϕ(x):=12x⊤Ax−b⊤x(x∈Rn). Then, with x⋆=A−1b, ϕ(x)−ϕ(x⋆)=12‖x−x⋆‖A2for every x∈Rn. In particular x⋆ is the unique minimizer of ϕ.

prp-spanning-tree-size.title: A Spanning Tree Has m - 1 Edges
prp-spanning-tree-size.title_html: A Spanning Tree Has m−1 Edges
prp-spanning-tree-size.html: Let G be a graph on m≥2 vertices. Every spanning tree of G has exactly m−1 edges. Conversely, if a set S of exactly m−1 edges is such that the graph on all m vertices with edge set S is connected, then S is a spanning tree.

prp-strassen-norm-bound.title: Strassen’s two-by-two product satisfies a norm bound
prp-strassen-norm-bound.title_html: Strassen’s two-by-two product satisfies a norm bound
prp-strassen-norm-bound.html: Let A,B∈M2(R) have representable entries, put α=maxi,j|aij| and β=maxi,j|bij|, and let C^ be the result of evaluating @thm-strassen with m=1, each Pk as written and each of the four combinations left to right. If 6u<1, then maxi,j|c^ij−(AB)ij| ≤ 12γ6αβ.

prp-toda-equations.title: The Toda Flow in Coordinates
prp-toda-equations.html: Let L∈Mn(R) be symmetric and tridiagonal, with diagonal entries d1,…,dn and off-diagonal entries e1,…,en−1, so ℓi,i+1=ℓi+1,i=ei. Put e0=en=0. Then [B(L),L] is again symmetric and tridiagonal, with [B(L),L]ii=2(ei2−ei−12),[B(L),L]i,i+1=ei(di+1−di). Consequently the Toda flow is the system di′=2(ei2−ei−12)  (1≤i≤n),ei′=ei(di+1−di)  (1≤i≤n−1).{#eq-toda-coordinates}

thm-arnoldi.title: The Arnoldi Process
thm-arnoldi.html:
Let A∈Mn(F), let b∈Fn be non-zero, let d=deg⁡mA,b, and run the Arnoldi process. Then the Arnoldi relation AQk=QkHk+hk+1,kqk+1ek⊤(1≤k≤d){#eq-arnoldi} holds, the last term being 0 when k=d. Moreover:

  1. For every j≤d, the list (q1,…,qj) is an orthonormal basis of Kj(A,b); moreover hj+1,j>0 for j<d, and hd+1,d=0, so the process breaks down at step d and at no earlier step.
  2. For 1≤k≤d we have Qk∗Qk=Ik, and Hk=Qk∗AQk is upper Hessenberg. For k<d, @eq-arnoldi can also be written AQk=Qk+1H~k.
  3. A breakdown means an invariant subspace: if hk+1,k=0, then AKk⊆Kk, and every eigenvalue of Hk is an eigenvalue of A.

thm-best-fitting-affine-subspace.title: The Best-Fitting Affine Subspace
thm-best-fitting-affine-subspace.html: Let x1,…,xN∈Rn have mean x¯ and centered data matrix Xc (@def-centered-data-matrix), let σ1≥σ2≥⋯≥0 be the singular values of Xc (@def-singular-values), and let u1,u2,… be the left singular vectors of a fixed singular value decomposition of Xc (@thm-svd). Let 1≤k≤min(n,N). Among all affine subspaces A⊆Rn of dimension at most k, the total squared distance D(A):=∑j=1Nd(xj,A)2 is smallest for A0=x¯+span(u1,…,uk), and its smallest value is ∑i>kσi2. Moreover every minimizing A contains x¯.

thm-cg-convergence.title: Convergence of Conjugate Gradients
thm-cg-convergence.html: Let A∈Mn(R) be symmetric positive definite with κ=κ2(A), let b∈Rn, and let x(k) be the conjugate gradient iterates from x(0), with x(k):=x⋆ once the iteration has terminated. Then for every k≥0, ‖x(k)−x⋆‖A ≤ 2(κ−1κ+1)k‖x(0)−x⋆‖A.

thm-cg-optimality.title: Conjugate Gradients: Orthogonality and Optimality
thm-cg-optimality.html:
Let A≻0, b∈Rn, x(0)∈Rn, and write Kk=Kk(A,r(0)) for the Krylov subspaces of @def-krylov-subspace, with K0={0}. Suppose the iteration of @def-conjugate-gradient has produced non-zero r(0),…,r(k). Then:

  1. p(0),…,p(k) are non-zero and pairwise A-orthogonal, and every αj and βj with j≤k is defined, with αj>0;
  2. r(0),…,r(k) are pairwise orthogonal, and (r(k+1))⊤p(j)=0 for every j≤k;
  3. span(r(0),…,r(k))=span(p(0),…,p(k))=Kk+1, a space of dimension k+1;
  4. x(k+1) is the unique minimizer of ‖x−x⋆‖A over the affine set x(0)+Kk+1.

thm-cholesky-stability.title: Cholesky Does Not Grow
thm-cholesky-stability.html:
Let A∈Mn(R) be symmetric positive definite with representable entries, and let L be its Cholesky factor, A=LL⊤ with ℓii>0 (@thm-cholesky).

  1. |ℓij|≤aii for all j≤i, and (|L||L⊤|)ik≤aiiakk≤maxp,q|apq|for all i,k.
  2. Suppose (n+1)u<1 and the recursion of Chapter 12 §02 runs to completion in the model, producing L^. Then L^L^⊤=A+ΔA,|ΔA|≤γn+1|L^||L^⊤|.
  3. If moreover γn+1<1, then maxi,j|Δaij|≤γn+11−γn+1maxi,j|aij|.

thm-elimination-is-schur-complements.title: Elimination Produces Schur Complements
thm-elimination-is-schur-complements.html: Let A∈Mn(F) and 1≤k≤n−1, and suppose the first k steps of elimination without row swaps (Chapter 2 §06) are carried out with non-zero pivots, producing A(k). Partition A=(AkBCD),A(k)=(VB′0S), with Ak,V∈Mk(F), the zero block being what the first k steps created. Then Ak is invertible and S=A/Ak=D−CAk−1B. In particular, for k=1 and a11≠0, one step of elimination replaces the trailing (n−1)×(n−1) block by the Schur complement of the 1×1 pivot block.

thm-fft-cost.title: The Cost of the Fast Fourier Transform
thm-fft-cost.title_html: The Cost of the Fast Fourier Transform
thm-fft-cost.html: Let C(n) be the number of operations the procedure above performs on an input of length n=2p, with p≥0. Then C(1)=0, C(2m)=2C(m)+3m−1(m≥1), and the solution of this recurrence is exactly C(2p)=32p2p−2p+1,that isC(n)=32nlog2⁡n−n+1. In particular C(n)=O(nlog⁡n).

thm-fft-factorization.title: The Radix-Two Factorization
thm-fft-factorization.html: Let n=2m with m≥1. Then Wn=Bn(Wm00Wm)Pn. Equivalently, for the unitary Fourier matrices, Fn=12Bn(Fm00Fm)Pn.

thm-forward-from-backward.title: Forward Error from Backward Error
thm-forward-from-backward.html: Let A∈Mn(C) be invertible, b≠0, and Ax=b. Let x^ be any vector which is the exact solution of a perturbed system, (A+ΔA)x^=b,‖ΔA‖‖A‖≤η, and suppose r:=κ(A)η<1. Then A+ΔA is invertible and ‖x^−x‖‖x‖≤r1−r=κ(A)η1−κ(A)η. In particular, if η=cu is admissible — as it is when the algorithm producing x^ is backward stable with constant c for the problem A↦A−1b with b held fixed, so that only A is perturbed — and if κ(A)cu≤12, then the forward relative error is at most 2κ(A)cu.

thm-growth-partial-pivoting.title: Growth Under Partial Pivoting
thm-growth-partial-pivoting.html: In exact arithmetic, elimination with partial pivoting on any A∈Mn(R) has growth factor gn≤2n−1.

thm-householder-backward-stable.title: Backward Stability of One Reflection
thm-householder-backward-stable.html:
Work in the model of @def-floating-point-model over R, and suppose (10m+16)u≤14. Let w∈Rm be non-zero and let H=Hw be the reflection of @def-householder-reflection, and suppose w and the input are stored exactly.

  1. For v∈Rm, let y^ be the vector computed from v and w by @eq-reflection-applied. Then y^=H(v+Δv),‖Δv‖2≤(10m+16)u‖v‖2.
  2. For A∈Mm×n(R), let B^ be the matrix whose columns are computed from those of A in this way. Then B^=H(A+ΔA),‖ΔA‖F≤(10m+16)u‖A‖F.

thm-inner-product-backward-error.title: Backward Error of an Inner Product
thm-inner-product-backward-error.title_html: Backward Error of an Inner Product
thm-inner-product-backward-error.html: Let x,y∈Rn have representable entries, let nu<1, and let the inner product be computed in the model of @def-floating-point-model in the natural order, s1=fl(x1y1),sk=fl(sk−1+fl(xkyk))(k=2,…,n). Then there is a vector Δx∈Rn with sn=(x+Δx)⊤yand|Δxi|≤γn|xi|  for every i.

thm-inverse-iteration.title: Inverse Iteration Converges to the Nearest Eigenvector
thm-inverse-iteration.title_html: Inverse Iteration Converges to the Nearest Eigenvector
thm-inverse-iteration.html: Let A∈Mn(F) be diagonalizable with eigenbasis v1,…,vn and eigenvalues λ1,…,λn, and let μ∈F be not an eigenvalue of A. Suppose there is an index j with |λj−μ|<|λi−μ|for every i≠j, so that λj is the unique eigenvalue nearest μ. Let x(0) be a unit vector whose vj-coefficient is non-zero. Then inverse iteration with shift μ is defined for every k, the iterates approach the eigenline span(vj) in the sense of @thm-power-method (a), and μk→λj, both at the rate ρμk, where ρμ=|λj−μ|mini≠j|λi−μ|<1.

thm-lanczos.title: The Lanczos Recurrence
thm-lanczos.html: Let A∈Mn(C) be Hermitian, let b≠0, and run the Arnoldi process. Then Hk is Hermitian for every k≤d, hence tridiagonal, with real diagonal entries; writing αj=hjj∈R and βj=hj+1,j, which is >0 for j<d and 0 for j=d, we have hj,j+1=βj and Aqj=βj−1qj−1+αjqj+βjqj+1(1≤j≤d),{#eq-lanczos} with β0q0 read as 0 and βdqd+1 as 0. Consequently Hk=Tk is the real symmetric tridiagonal matrix with diagonal (α1,…,αk) and off-diagonal (β1,…,βk−1), and each step of the process needs only qj−1 and qj.

thm-laplacian-kernel.title: The Kernel of the Laplacian
thm-laplacian-kernel.html: Let G be a graph on m vertices with k≥1 edges, with components C1,…,Cc, and let 1Cr∈Rm be the vector with entry 1 at the vertices of Cr and 0 elsewhere. Then nul(L)=span(1C1,…,1Cc), this list is a basis, and the eigenvalue 0 of L has multiplicity exactly c. In particular L is singular, and nul(L)=span(1) exactly when G is connected.

thm-lax-isospectral.title: Lax Pairs Are Isospectral
thm-lax-isospectral.html: Let (L,B) be a Lax pair on an open interval I. Then the characteristic polynomial of L(t) does not depend on t: pL(t)=pL(s)for all s,t∈I. In particular L(t) has the same eigenvalues as L(s), with the same algebraic multiplicities, and trL(t) and detL(t) are constant.

thm-least-squares-conditioning.title: Conditioning of the Least-Squares Problem
thm-least-squares-conditioning.html:
Let A∈Mm×n(F) have rank n≤m, let b≠0, let x be the least-squares solution of Az=b, and let θ<π/2 be as in @eq-ls-angle. Let E∈Mm×n(F) and f∈Fm, and for real t near 0 let x(t) be the least-squares solution of (A+tE)z=b+tf. Then x(t) is defined and differentiable near t=0, with x(0)=x, and

‖x′(0)‖‖x‖ ≤ κ2(A)(εA+εbcos⁡θ) + κ2(A)2εAtan⁡θ,

where εA=‖E‖/‖A‖ and εb=‖f‖/‖b‖.

thm-lu-backward-error.title: Backward Error of a Factorization
thm-lu-backward-error.html: Let A∈Mn(R) have representable entries, let nu<1, and suppose the algorithm above runs to completion in the model of @def-floating-point-model, producing L^ and U^. Then L^U^=A+ΔAwith|ΔA|≤γn|L^||U^| entrywise.

thm-matrix-tree.title: Matrix-Tree Theorem
thm-matrix-tree.html: Let G be a graph on m≥2 vertices with k≥1 edges and Laplacian L. Fix a vertex r, and let L0=LI,I∈Mm−1(R) be L with the row and the column of r deleted, where I=[m]∖{r}. Then detL0=#{spanning trees of G}. In particular the answer does not depend on which vertex r is deleted, and detL0=0 exactly when G is disconnected.

thm-normal-equations-lose-twice.title: The Normal Equations Lose Twice the Digits
thm-normal-equations-lose-twice.title_html: The Normal Equations Lose Twice the Digits
thm-normal-equations-lose-twice.html:
Let A∈Mm×n(F) have rank n≤m, let b≠0, let x be the least-squares solution and let θ<π/2 be as in @eq-ls-angle. Work in the model of @def-floating-point-model, and suppose mu≤12.

  1. (Normal equations.) Suppose C=fl(A∗A) and d=fl(A∗b) are formed by inner products, and that Cz=d is then solved by a method that is backward stable in the sense of @def-backward-stable, so that the computed x^ satisfies (C+ΔC)x^=d+Δd with ‖ΔC‖≤csu‖C‖ and ‖Δd‖≤csu‖d‖. Then there is a constant c, depending only on m, n and cs and of size O(mn), such that if cuκ2(A)2<1 then ‖x^−x‖‖x‖ ≤ cuκ2(A)2(1+1cos⁡θ)1−cuκ2(A)2. The bound carries κ2(A)2 even when the residual is zero.
  2. (A backward stable least-squares solver.) Suppose instead that x^ is the exact least-squares solution of (A+ΔA)z=b+Δb for some ΔA,Δb with ‖ΔA‖≤c′u‖A‖ and ‖Δb‖≤c′u‖b‖. Then, to first order in u as in @eq-ls-first-order, ‖x^−x‖‖x‖ ≲ c′u[κ2(A)(1+1cos⁡θ)+κ2(A)2tan⁡θ].

thm-normal-modes.title: Normal Modes
thm-normal-modes.html:
Let (M,K) be a mass–spring system with n degrees of freedom (@def-mass-spring-system).

  1. For ω∈R and v∈Rn with v≠0, the complex-valued function x(t)=eiωtv satisfies @eq-mass-spring if and only if Kv=ω2Mv.
  2. There are real numbers 0≤ω1≤⋯≤ωn and vectors v1,…,vn∈Rn with Kvj=ωj2Mvjandvi⊤Mvj=δij, and (v1,…,vn) is a basis of Rn.
  3. Every motion of the system is x(t)=∑j=1ncj(t)vj, where cj(t)={ajcos⁡ωjt+bjsin⁡ωjt,ωj>0,aj+bjt,ωj=0, for uniquely determined real aj,bj; conversely every such function is a motion. The coefficients are aj=vj⊤Mx(0), and bj=vj⊤Mx′(0)/ωj when ωj>0, bj=vj⊤Mx′(0) when ωj=0.

The numbers ωj do not depend on the construction in (b): by @thm-generalized-eigenvalues-real (b) the ωj2 are exactly the roots of det(K−λM), with multiplicity. They are the natural frequencies, and the pairs (ωj,vj) are the normal modes of the system.

thm-power-method.title: The Power Method
thm-power-method.html:
Let A∈Mn(F) be diagonalizable, with a basis v1,…,vn of eigenvectors, Avi=λivi, ordered by modulus so that |λ1|>|λ2|≥⋯≥|λn|. Let x(0)=c1v1+⋯+cnvn be a unit vector with c1≠0, and put ρ=|λ2/λ1|<1, q1=v1/‖v1‖ and C=1‖v1‖∑i≥2|cic1|‖vi‖. Then the power iteration of @def-power-iteration is defined for every k, and for every k with Cρk≤12 there is a scalar ωk of modulus 1 with

  1. ‖ωkx(k)−q1‖≤4Cρk;
  2. |μk−λ1|≤8‖A‖Cρk.

In particular μk→λ1, and the iterates approach the eigenline span(v1) in the sense of (a), both at the rate ρk.

thm-qr-convergence.title: Convergence of the First Column
thm-qr-convergence.html: Let A∈Mn(C) be invertible and diagonalizable, say A=XΛX−1 with Λ=diag(λ1,…,λn) and with v1,…,vn the columns of X. Assume a single dominant eigenvalue, |λ1|>|λ2|≥⋯≥|λn|>0, and write e1=c1v1+⋯+cnvn, assuming c1≠0. Put t=|λ2/λ1|<1. Then there is a constant C, depending on A and X but not on k, such that the unshifted QR iterates satisfy ‖A(k+1)e1−λ1e1‖2≤Ctk(k≥1). In particular a11(k)→λ1 and ai1(k)→0 for every i≥2, each at the rate tk. For n=2 this says that the iterates converge to upper triangular form, with a11(k)→λ1 and a22(k)→λ2.

thm-qr-is-orthogonal-iteration.title: QR Iterates Factor the Powers
thm-qr-is-orthogonal-iteration.html: Let A∈Mn(F) and let A(k), Q(k), R(k) be as in @def-qr-iteration. Then for every k≥1, A(k+1)=Uk∗AUkandAk=UkTk. In particular UkTk is a QR factorization of Ak.

thm-ritz-extreme-convergence.title: A Rate for the Largest Ritz Value
thm-ritz-extreme-convergence.title_html: A Rate for the Largest Ritz Value
thm-ritz-extreme-convergence.html: Let A∈Mn(C) be Hermitian with eigenvalues λ1>λ2≥⋯≥λn and an orthonormal eigenbasis v1,…,vn. Let b be a unit vector with b=∑icivi and c1≠0, and put τ2=∑i≥2|ci|2|c1|2,ρ=λ2−λn2λ1−λ2−λn∈[0,1). Then the largest Ritz value θ1(k) from Kk(A,b) satisfies, for 1≤k≤d, 0 ≤ λ1−θ1(k) ≤ (λ1−λn)τ2ρ2(k−1), and θ1(k) is non-decreasing in k.

thm-ritz-interlacing.title: Ritz Values Interlace, and Their Residual Is One Number
thm-ritz-interlacing.title_html: Ritz Values Interlace, and Their Residual Is One Number
thm-ritz-interlacing.html:
Let A∈Mn(C) be Hermitian with eigenvalues λ1(A)≥⋯≥λn(A), let 1≤k≤d, and let θ1≥⋯≥θk be the Ritz values from Kk(A,b), that is, the eigenvalues of Tk.

  1. λi(A) ≥ θi ≥ λi+n−k(A) for 1≤i≤k.
  2. If Tky=θy with ‖y‖=1 and x=Qky, then Ax−θx=βkykqk+1,so‖Ax−θx‖=βk|yk|, where yk is the last coordinate of y and βk=hk+1,k, with βdqd+1 read as 0.

thm-rqi-cubic.title: Rayleigh Quotient Iteration Converges Cubically
thm-rqi-cubic.html:
Let A∈Mn(F) be Hermitian with an orthonormal basis q1,…,qn of eigenvectors, Aqi=λiqi, and fix an index j whose eigenvalue is simple. Put g=mini≠j|λi−λj|>0,D=maxi≠j|λi−λj|, and for a unit vector x write s(x)=‖x−qjqj∗x‖, the length of the part of x orthogonal to qj.

Let x=x(k) be a unit iterate with s=s(x) satisfying s≤12 and Ds2≤g2. Then |μk−λj|≤Ds2, and either μk=λj — the iteration has found the eigenvalue exactly — or the next iterate is defined and s(x(k+1)) ≤ 4Dgs3. Consequently, if s0=s(x(0)) satisfies s0≤12 and s02≤g/(8D), then ak:=4D/gs(x(k)) satisfies ak≤a03k with a0≤1/2, so s(x(k))→0 and μk→λj.

thm-steepest-descent.title: Convergence of Steepest Descent
thm-steepest-descent.html: Let A∈Mn(R) be symmetric positive definite with κ=κ2(A), let b∈Rn, and let x(0),x(1),… be the steepest descent iterates. Then for every k for which x(k) is defined, ‖x(k)−x⋆‖A≤(κ−1κ+1)k‖x(0)−x⋆‖A.

thm-strassen.title: Strassen’s identity
thm-strassen.html: Let F be a field, let m≥1, and let A,B∈M2m(F) be partitioned into m×m blocks, A=(A11A12A21A22),B=(B11B12B21B22). Define seven products P1=(A11+A22)(B11+B22),P2=(A21+A22)B11,P3=A11(B12−B22),P4=A22(B21−B11),P5=(A11+A12)B22,P6=(A21−A11)(B11+B12),P7=(A12−A22)(B21+B22). Then, with the same block partition of AB, AB=(P1+P4−P5+P7P3+P5P2+P4P1+P3−P2+P6). Only seven products of m×m matrices occur on the right, where @thm-block-multiplication asks for eight.

thm-strassen-cost.title: The cost of the recursion
thm-strassen-cost.html: Let n=2p with p≥0. Applying @thm-strassen recursively, with the 1×1 case done by a single multiplication, multiplies two matrices in Mn(F) with exactly T(n)=7nlog2⁡7−6n2 arithmetic operations. In particular T(n)=O(nlog2⁡7) and ω≤log2⁡7=2.8073….

thm-strassen-not-entrywise-stable.title: Strassen’s algorithm has no useful entrywise error bound
thm-strassen-not-entrywise-stable.title_html: Strassen’s algorithm has no useful entrywise error bound
thm-strassen-not-entrywise-stable.html: Work in a model as in @def-floating-point-model, and suppose the set R of representable numbers contains a number ε with ε>0,1+ε∈R,ε2∈R,fl((1+ε)2)=1+2ε. Put A=B=diag(1,ε). Then the C^ of @prp-strassen-norm-bound has c^22=0, while (AB)22=ε2. Consequently, any constant c for which |C^−AB| ≤ cu|A||B| holds entrywise for this A and B must satisfy c≥1/u.

thm-toda-qr-connection.title: One QR Step Is One Unit of Toda Time
thm-toda-qr-connection.title_html: One QR Step Is One Unit of Toda Time
thm-toda-qr-connection.html:
Let L0∈Mn(R) be symmetric and let A(1),A(2),A(3),… be the unshifted QR iterates of @def-qr-iteration started at A(1)=eL0, with the factorizations A(k)=Q(k)R(k),A(k+1)=R(k)Q(k)(k≥1) normalized so that each R(k) has positive diagonal entries, and write Wk=Q(1)Q(2)⋯Q(k), with W0=I. Then for every k≥0:

  1. the factorizations exist and are unique, and A(k+1)=Wk⊤A(1)Wk;
  2. Wk is the orthogonal factor in the QR factorization of ekL0;
  3. A(k+1)=eLk, where Lk=Wk⊤L0Wk is symmetric and has the same eigenvalues as L0.

thm-triangular-solve-backward-error.title: Backward Error of a Triangular Solve
thm-triangular-solve-backward-error.title_html: Backward Error of a Triangular Solve
thm-triangular-solve-backward-error.html: Let T∈Mn(R) be lower triangular with representable entries and non-zero diagonal, let b∈Rn be representable, and let nu<1. Let x^ be computed by forward substitution in the model: for each i, the products tijx^j are subtracted from bi one at a time in increasing order of j, and the result is divided by tii — that is, exactly the computation of @lem-substitution-row with m=i−1. Then there is a lower triangular ΔT with (T+ΔT)x^=band|Δtij|≤γi|tij|≤γn|tij|(j≤i). The same statement, with γn+1−i in place of γi, holds for back substitution with an upper triangular T.

thm-variance-explained.title: Variance Captured by the Principal Directions
thm-variance-explained.title_html: Variance Captured by the Principal Directions
thm-variance-explained.html:
In the situation of @prp-covariance-and-svd, let 1≤k≤min(n,N), let U0=span(u1,…,uk) and let P be the orthogonal projection onto a subspace U with dim⁡U≤k. Write var(U):=1N∑j=1N‖P(xj−x¯)‖2. Then:

  1. var(U) is the total variance of the projected points Px1,…,PxN, whose mean is Px¯;
  2. var(U)+1ND(x¯+U)=trS, where D is as in @thm-best-fitting-affine-subspace;
  3. var(U)≤var(U0)=1N∑i≤kσi2;
  4. if Xc≠0, the fraction of the total variance captured by U0 is var(U0)trS=σ12+⋯+σk2σ12+σ22+….
